This codebase is Flask 3.2.0.dev (`pyproject.toml:3`), where the former `RequestContext` has merged into `AppContext` (`CHANGES.rst:8-11`). A single `AppContext` object now serves as both the app and request context; `RequestContext` survives only as a deprecated module-level alias (`src/flask/ctx.py:527-538`).

Context creation.** `wsgi_app` calls `self.request_context(environ)` (`src/flask/app.py:1592` → `src/flask/app.py:1501-1515`), which is `AppContext.from_environ` (`src/flask/ctx.py:340-348`): it builds the `Request` from the environ (`app.request_class(environ)`, `src/flask/ctx.py:346`) and attaches the app's JSON module (`:347`). Inside `AppContext.__init__` (`src/flask/ctx.py:300-337`):
- `self.g` is a fresh `_AppCtxGlobals` namespace (`src/flask/ctx.py:312`, class default at `src/flask/sansio/app.py:182`)
- `self.url_adapter` is bound to the request environ via `app.create_url_adapter` (`src/flask/ctx.py:326`), which calls `url_map.bind_to_environ` (`src/flask/app.py:548`). If binding raises an `HTTPException`, it is stored as `request.routing_exception` (`src/flask/ctx.py:327-329`)
- `_cv_token = None` and `_push_count = 0` are initialized (`src/flask/ctx.py:331-334`)

At this point nothing is "active": the `ContextVar` `_cv_app` (`src/flask/globals.py:40`) is unset, so every proxy (`current_app`, `g`, `request`, `session`) raises `RuntimeError` (`src/flask/globals.py:28-62`).

**3. Context push.** `ctx.push()` (`src/flask/app.py:1596` → `src/flask/ctx.py:416-444`) increments `_push_count` (`:428`), then on first push sets the ContextVar (`_cv_app.set(self)`, `:433`), sends `appcontext_pushed` (`:434`), opens the session (`self._get_session()`, `:439` → `session_interface.open_session` at `:388`, with a null-session fallback at `:391`), and matches the URL (`self.match_request()`, `:444` → `url_adapter.match(return_rule=True)` at `:410`, storing `url_rule`/`view_args` on success at `:414` or a `routing_exception` at `:412`).

Dispatch.** `full_dispatch_request(ctx)` (`src/flask/app.py:992-1019`) sets `_got_first_request` (`:1010`), sends `request_started` (`:1013`), runs `preprocess_request` (`:1014`, defined at `:1366` — url value preprocessors at `:1381`, then `before_request` functions at `:1386`), then `dispatch_request` (`:1016`, defined at `:966`): it re-raises any stored routing exception (`:978-979`), answers automatic `OPTIONS` (`:987`), and otherwise calls `view_functions[rule.endpoint](**view_args)` (`:990`). Exceptions go to `handle_user_exception` (`:1017-1018`, defined at `:865`); unhandled ones reach `wsgi_app`'s `except Exception` (`:1598-1600`) → `handle_exception` (defined at `:897`), which sends `got_request_exception` (`:926`) and builds a 500 response.

**5. Response finalization.** `finalize_request` (`src/flask/app.py:1021-1050`) converts the return value with `make_response` (`:1039`, defined at `:1224`), runs `process_response` (`:1041`, defined at `:1394`): `after_this_request` functions (`:1407`), then `after_request` functions in reverse registration order per blueprint then app (`:1410-1412`), then `save_session` unless the session is null (`:1415-1416`). Finally it sends `request_finished` with the response (`:1042-1044`).

**6. Context pop.** Back in `wsgi_app`, the response is called as a WSGI app (`return response(environ, start_response)`, `src/flask/app.py:1604`), and the `finally` block pops the context with any captured error: `ctx.pop(error)` (`:1616`). `pop()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:446-504`) verifies it is the active context, decrements `_push_count` (`:481`), and on the final pop runs `do_teardown_request(self, exc)` (`:490`), closes the request (`:493`), runs `do_teardown_appcontext(self, exc)` (`:496`), resets the ContextVar (`_cv_app.reset`, `:498`), sends `appcontext_popped` (`:501-502`), and raises any collected teardown errors together (`:504`). ## Subquestion 1: The context object and what becomes available at each stage

A single **`AppContext`** is created per request (via `AppContext.from_environ`, `src/flask/ctx.py:340-348`) and made active by `_cv_app.set(self)` inside `push()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:433`). Its "request context" nature is just the presence of `_request` (`has_request` property, `src/flask/ctx.py:351-353`).

Objects available per stage:

| Stage | Newly available |
|---|---|
| Creation (`ctx.py:300-337`) | Nothing proxied yet; the raw `Request`, `g` namespace, and bound `url_adapter` (or `routing_exception`) exist only inside the context object |
| After `_cv_app.set` (`ctx.py:433`) | `app_ctx`, `current_app`, `g` proxies (`src/flask/globals.py:41-49`); the `request` proxy also resolves now, since `_request` was set at construction (`src/flask/ctx.py:370-379`) |
| After session opening (`ctx.py:439`) | `session` proxy (`src/flask/globals.py:60-62`). Note `push()` calls `_get_session()` directly, bypassing the `session` property, so `accessed` is not yet `True` (`ctx.py:402`) — that only happens when user code touches `flask.session` |
| After URL matching (`ctx.py:444`) | `request.url_rule`, `request.view_args` (`ctx.py:414`), hence `request.endpoint` (`src/flask/wrappers.py:147`) and `request.blueprints` (`:181`) |
| After `_cv_app.reset` in `pop()` (`ctx.py:498`) | All proxies raise `RuntimeError` again; `has_request_context()`/`has_app_context()` return `False` (`src/flask/ctx.py:209-232`) |

Other context-dependent state: `after_this_request` appends to `ctx._after_request_functions` (`src/flask/ctx.py:147`), consumed during finalization (`src/flask/app.py:1407`); flashed messages cache in `ctx._flashes` (`src/flask/helpers.py:391-394`).

One documentation inconsistency worth flagging: the class docstring claims "The session is loaded the first time it is accessed, rather than when the context is pushed" (`src/flask/ctx.py:295-297`), but `push()` unconditionally opens it for request contexts (`src/flask/ctx.py:436-439`), with an inline comment stating this is so a custom `open_session` can use the request context. The code (and its intent comment at `:442-443`) is authoritative for an ordinary WSGI request: the session opens during push.

## Subquestion 2: Actual order of the five operations

For an ordinary request, the order is:

1. **`appcontext_pushed` signal** — `src/flask/ctx.py:434`, immediately after the ContextVar set at `:433`, still inside `push()`
2. **Session opening** — `src/flask/ctx.py:439` (`open_session` at `:388`)
3. **URL matching** — `src/flask/ctx.py:444` (`match` at `:410`), deliberately after the session "so that the session is available in custom URL converters" (comment at `:442-443`); `tests/test_session_interface.py:16-18` confirms that during `open_session` matching has not yet run, since the test must call `app_ctx.match_request()` manually
4. **`request_started` signal** — `src/flask/app.py:1013`, the first statement of `full_dispatch_request`, i.e. after `push()` has fully returned
5. **`request_finished` signal** — `src/flask/app.py:1042-1044`, inside `finalize_request` after `process_response`, before the response is returned

So: **app-context push signaling → session opening → URL matching → request-start signaling → (preprocess/dispatch/view) → request-finished signaling**. The two non-obvious facts are that URL matching happens *inside* `push()` (before `request_started` is ever sent) and that session opening precedes matching.

## Subquestion 3: Repeated pushes, and the operation that passes an exception into cleanup

**Repeated pushes.** `push()` increments `_push_count` on every call (`src/flask/ctx.py:428`), but if `_cv_token` is already set it returns early (`:430-431`). So a nested push of the same context sends no second `appcontext_pushed`, does not reopen the session, and does not re-run URL matching. Symmetrically, `pop()` decrements `_push_count` (`:481`) and returns early while it is above zero (`:483-484`): teardown functions, `request.close()`, `do_teardown_appcontext`, the ContextVar reset, and `appcontext_popped` run only when the outermost pop brings the count to zero; until then the context stays the active context (`src/flask/ctx.py:446-504`). This is what lets `stream_with_context` work: it re-enters the context inside the generator via `with ctx:` (`src/flask/helpers.py:133`, primed by `next(wrapped_g)` at `:146-147`), so the `finally`-block pop in `wsgi_app` only decrements and real cleanup is deferred until the stream is consumed. The debug/test preservation hook (`src/flask/app.py:1606-1608`) relies on the same counting. (Related but distinct: `copy_current_request_context` creates a *copy* sharing the same request/session objects, `src/flask/ctx.py:359-367`, pushed in a `with` block at `src/flask/helpers.py:203`.)

**Exception into cleanup.** The responsible operation is **`Flask.wsgi_app` passing the captured `error` to `ctx.pop(error)` in its `finally` block** (`src/flask/app.py:1616`). `error` is captured from the `except Exception as e` clause (`:1599`) or, for a `BaseException` such as `KeyboardInterrupt`, from the bare `except` that records `sys.exc_info()[1]` and re-raises (`:1601-1603`); the deprecated `should_ignore_error` hook can null it first (`:1609-1614`). Inside `pop(exc)`, that exception is forwarded to `do_teardown_request(self, exc)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:490`) and `do_teardown_appcontext(self, exc)` (`:496`), which hand it to every teardown function (`src/flask/app.py:1446, 1473`) and to the `request_tearing_down`/`appcontext_tearing_down` signals (`src/flask/app.py:1449, 1477`). The same mechanism exists for manual `with` usage via `AppContext.__exit__`, which passes `exc_value` to `pop()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:516`). Note that even exceptions converted into a 500 response by `handle_exception` still reach teardown this way, because `wsgi_app` sets `error` before producing the error response. In 3.2, all teardown callbacks run even when some raise; errors are collected by `_CollectErrors` (`src/flask/helpers.py:654-656`) and raised together afterward (`src/flask/ctx.py:486-504`).

| # | Subquestion | Confidence | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Context object created/activated and objects available per stage | High | Direct reading of `ctx.py`, `globals.py`, `app.py`; corroborated by `tests/test_reqctx.py:123-145`. Minor caveat: stale docstring at `ctx.py:295-297` vs. actual eager session open at `ctx.py:436-439`; I reported the code behavior |
| 2 | Order of session opening, app-context push signal, URL matching, request-start, request-finished | High | Unambiguous statement order in `ctx.py:433-444` and `app.py:1013, 1042`; intent comment at `ctx.py:442-443`; `tests/test_session_interface.py:6-33` corroborates session-before-matching |
| 3 | Behavior of repeated pushes; operation passing the exception into cleanup | High | `_push_count`/`_cv_token` logic at `ctx.py:428-431, 481-484` read directly; `stream_with_context` at `helpers.py:133, 146-147` exercises it; exception path at `app.py:1598-1616` → `ctx.py:490, 496` read directly and matched by `tests/test_reqctx.py:16-27, 205-224` |

The only soft spot is the session-timing docstring discrepancy noted under subquestion 1; everything else is confirmed by both the source and the test suite.

- `self.g = app.app_ctx_globals_class()` is created (`src/flask/ctx.py:312`),
- `app.create_url_adapter(request)` binds the URL map to the environ, applying `TRUSTED_HOSTS`/`SERVER_NAME`/subdomain rules (`src/flask/ctx.py:326`; `src/flask/app.py:509-552`); if binding raises an `HTTPException`, it is stashed as `request.routing_exception` (`src/flask/ctx.py:327-330`),

Nothing is proxied yet: `_cv_app` has not been set, so `flask.current_app`/`g`/`request`/`session` would raise.

- `_cv_token = _cv_app.set(self)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:433`) — from this moment `app_ctx`, `current_app`, `g`, and `request` proxies resolve, because they are `LocalProxy`s over the single `_cv_app` `ContextVar` (`src/flask/globals.py:40-62`),
- `appcontext_pushed` signal is sent (`src/flask/ctx.py:434`),
- because this context has request data: the session is opened eagerly via `_get_session()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:437-439`), which calls `session_interface.open_session(app, request)` and falls back to `make_null_session` if it returns `None` (`src/flask/ctx.py:381-393`) — now `session` is usable,
- then URL matching runs, deliberately *after* session loading "so that the session is available in custom URL converters" (`src/flask/ctx.py:441-444`). `match_request()` calls `url_adapter.match(return_rule=True)` and stores either the `(url_rule, view_args)` pair or a `routing_exception` on the request (`src/flask/ctx.py:405-414`). After this, `request.endpoint` and `request.blueprint` become non-`None` (`src/flask/wrappers.py:147-163`).

- sends the `request_started` signal (`src/flask/app.py:1013`),
- runs `preprocess_request`: `url_value_preprocessors` then `before_request` functions per blueprint; a non-`None` return short-circuits the view (`src/flask/app.py:1366-1391`),
- calls `dispatch_request(ctx)` (`src/flask/app.py:966-990`): if `req.routing_exception` is set it is raised via `raise_routing_exception` (`src/flask/app.py:978-979`); automatic `OPTIONS` handling; otherwise the matched view function is invoked with `view_args` (`src/flask/app.py:990`),

- `make_response(rv)` converts the view return value (`src/flask/app.py:1039`),
- `process_response` runs `after_this_request` functions (`ctx._after_request_functions`), then `after_request` functions in reverse registration order per blueprint then app, and saves the session via `session_interface.save_session` unless it's a null session (`src/flask/app.py:1041`; `src/flask/app.py:1394-1417`),
- the `request_finished` signal is sent with the response (`src/flask/app.py:1042-1044`).

- `do_teardown_request(self, exc)` — all `teardown_request`/blueprint callbacks plus the `request_tearing_down` signal, each receiving `exc` (`src/flask/ctx.py:490`; `src/flask/app.py:1420-1451`),
- `request.close()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:493`),
- `do_teardown_appcontext(self, exc)` — `teardown_appcontext` callbacks plus `appcontext_tearing_down`, again with `exc` (`src/flask/ctx.py:496`; `src/flask/app.py:1453-1479`),
- `_cv_app.reset(self._cv_token)` and `_cv_token = None` — the proxies stop resolving (`src/flask/ctx.py:498-499`),
- `appcontext_popped` signal (`src/flask/ctx.py:502`); errors accumulated during teardown are collected and raised together (`src/flask/ctx.py:486-504`).

---

## 1. Which context object, and what is available when

The context is a single **`AppContext` carrying request data**. Since 3.2, `RequestContext` has merged into `AppContext` and survives only as a deprecated alias (`src/flask/ctx.py:528-541`; `CHANGES.rst:8-13`). A per-request context is created by `Flask.request_context` → `AppContext.from_environ` (`src/flask/app.py:1501-1515`).

| Stage | Available |
|---|---|
| Created, before push | Only direct attributes: `ctx.app`, `ctx.request`, `ctx.g`, `ctx.url_adapter` (possibly `None`), `request.routing_exception` if URL binding failed. No proxies work (`_cv_app` unset). |
| Pushed (`_cv_app.set`, `ctx.py:433`) | `current_app`, `g`, `app_ctx`, and `request` proxies resolve (`globals.py:40-62`) |
| Session opened (`ctx.py:439`) | `session` proxy resolves (`globals.py:60`); `session.accessed` set on proxy use (`ctx.py:396-402`) |
| URL matched (`ctx.py:444`) | `request.url_rule`, `request.view_args` (`ctx.py:414`), hence `request.endpoint`, `request.blueprint` (`wrappers.py:147-163`); `before_request`/view dispatch proceed |
| Popped (`ctx.py:498-499`) | All proxies stop resolving; `request`/`session` raise `RuntimeError` ("There is no request in this context", `ctx.py:373-374,383-384`) |

## 2. Actual order of the five operations

1. **App-context push signaling** — `appcontext_pushed.send` inside `push()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:434`)
2. **Session opening** — `_get_session()` → `open_session` inside `push()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:439,388`)
3. **URL matching** — `match_request()` at the end of `push()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:444,410`)
4. **Request-start signaling** — `request_started.send` at the top of `full_dispatch_request` (`src/flask/app.py:1013`)
5. **Request-finished signaling** — `request_finished.send` in `finalize_request`, after `process_response` (`src/flask/app.py:1042`)

So three of the five (1-3) all happen *inside* `push()`, before dispatch begins; the session is deliberately opened before matching so custom URL converters can use it (`src/flask/ctx.py:441-443`). One doc inconsistency worth noting: the `AppContext` docstring claims the session "is loaded the first time it is accessed, rather than when the context is pushed" (`src/flask/ctx.py:295-297`), but the code opens it eagerly during `push()`; the code is authoritative here (the property at `ctx.py:396-402` only provides lazy opening as a fallback).

## 3. Re-pushing the same context, and the exception-passing operation

**Re-push behavior.** `_push_count` tracks nested pushes; cleanup runs only after the original push is popped (`src/flask/ctx.py:334-337`). On a second `push()`, the count increments (`src/flask/ctx.py:428`) but the method returns early because `_cv_token is not None` (`src/flask/ctx.py:430-431`). Consequently, the second push does **not** re-set the contextvar, re-send `appcontext_pushed`, re-open the session, or re-run URL matching — the docstring states it "will only trigger matching and signals if it is not currently pushed" (`src/flask/ctx.py:424-425`). Symmetrically, `pop()` decrements the count (`src/flask/ctx.py:481`) and returns without any cleanup while `_push_count > 0` (`src/flask/ctx.py:483-484`); until the count reaches zero the context *remains the active context* (`src/flask/ctx.py:454-457`). This nesting is what supports streaming and test-client context preservation.

**The exception-passing operation.** It is **`AppContext.pop(exc)`** — its `exc` parameter, documented as "An unhandled exception that was raised while the context was active. Passed to teardown functions." (`src/flask/ctx.py:446,459-461`). `pop` forwards `exc` to `do_teardown_request(self, exc)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:490`) and `do_teardown_appcontext(self, exc)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:496`), which hand it to every teardown callback (`src/flask/app.py:1446,1474`) and to the `request_tearing_down`/`appcontext_tearing_down` signals (`src/flask/app.py:1449,1477`). In the WSGI path, `wsgi_app` captures the failure as `error = e` (`src/flask/app.py:1599`) and passes it via `ctx.pop(error)` in the `finally` block (`src/flask/app.py:1616`); when the context is managed with `with`, `__exit__` does the same via `self.pop(exc_value)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:510-516`).

---

|---|---|---|
| 1. Context object (`AppContext` with request data) and per-stage availability | High | Direct reads of `ctx.py:300-348,416-444`, `globals.py:40-62`, `wrappers.py:147-163`; only the session-loading docstring contradiction (`ctx.py:295-297` vs `ctx.py:439`) required judgment, and I reported both. |

## 2. Actual order of the five operations

1. **App-context push signaling** — `appcontext_pushed.send` in `push()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:434`), immediately after `_cv_app.set` (`:433`).
2. **Session opening** — `self._get_session()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:441`), inside `push()`, after the signal.
3. **URL matching** — `self.match_request()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:445`), inside `push()`, deliberately after the session so "the session is available in custom URL converters" (comment at `:443-444`).
4. **Request-start signaling** — `request_started.send` (`src/flask/app.py:1013`), the first thing `full_dispatch_request` does, i.e. after `push()` has returned.
5. **Request-finished signaling** — `request_finished.send` (`src/flask/app.py:1042`), after `process_response` (which itself saves the session at `src/flask/app.py:1416`).

So: **push signal → session open → URL match → request_started → (before_request, view, make_response, after_request+save_session) → request_finished**.

**What changes on a second push — almost nothing, by design.** `push()` increments `_push_count` (`src/flask/ctx.py:428`) and returns immediately if `self._cv_token is not None` (`:430-431`). Symmetrically, `pop()` decrements `_push_count` (`:481`) and returns early while `_push_count > 0` (`:483-484`), so teardown, `request.close()`, the ContextVar reset, and `appcontext_popped` only run on the pop that brings the count to zero — "it will remain the active context" until then (`:452-454`). This is what makes nested `with ctx:` blocks, streaming, and `copy_current_request_context` (`src/flask/ctx.py:199-244`) safe.

**The operation responsible for passing an exception into cleanup is the context pop, specifically `ctx.pop(error)`.** Two paths funnel into it:

- WSGI path: `wsgi_app`'s `finally` block calls `ctx.pop(error)` (`src/flask/app.py:1616`), where `error` was captured by `except Exception as e: error = e` (`:1599`) or the bare `except: error = sys.exc_info()[1]` (`:1602`) for non-`Exception` throwables. `should_ignore_error` may null it first (`:1610-1614`).
- `with`-block path: `AppContext.__exit__` calls `self.pop(exc_value)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:516`), forwarding whatever exception propagated through the block.

Inside `pop(exc)`, that exception is delivered to cleanup: `self.app.do_teardown_request(self, exc)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:490`) and `self.app.do_teardown_appcontext(self, exc)` (`:496`), which pass `exc` to every `teardown_request`/`teardown_appcontext` function and to the `request_tearing_down` (`src/flask/app.py:1449`) and `appcontext_tearing_down` (`src/flask/app.py:1477`) signals. That is the sole channel by which an unhandled exception reaches teardown code; `full_dispatch_request` never passes exceptions forward, it converts them via `handle_user_exception`/`handle_exception` (`src/flask/app.py:1018-1019`, `:948`).

| 3. Second push: `_push_count`/`_cv_token` guard; no duplicate signals, session open, or matching; cleanup only on final pop | High | `ctx.py:428-431, 481-484` plus docstrings at `:427-428, 452-454` |
| 3. `ctx.pop(error)` (and `__exit__` → `pop(exc_value)`) is the operation passing exceptions into teardown | High | `app.py:1599-1616`, `ctx.py:490,496,516`, `app.py:1449,1477` |

This repo is Flask 3.2.0.dev (`pyproject.toml:3`), where `RequestContext` has been merged into `AppContext` (`CHANGES.rst:8-10`). A request is handled by a single combined context object. Here is the trace, followed by the three subquestions.

## The trace

**Entry.** The WSGI server calls `Flask.__call__` (`src/flask/app.py:1618`), which delegates to `wsgi_app` (`src/flask/app.py:1566`).

**Context creation.** `wsgi_app` builds the context immediately: `ctx = self.request_context(environ)` (`src/flask/app.py:1592`), which returns `AppContext.from_environ(self, environ)` (`src/flask/app.py:1515`). `from_environ` constructs the request object (`request = app.request_class(environ)`) and binds the JSON provider to it (`src/flask/ctx.py:346-348`). The `AppContext.__init__` then (`src/flask/ctx.py:300`):
- stores the app (`self.app`, `src/flask/ctx.py:307`) and creates `g` via `app.app_ctx_globals_class()` (default `_AppCtxGlobals`, `src/flask/ctx.py:312`; `src/flask/sansio/app.py:182`);
- stores the request and a lazy `_session = None` (`src/flask/ctx.py:320-321`);
- binds the URL adapter via `app.create_url_adapter(request)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:326`), which calls `url_map.bind_to_environ(...)` (`src/flask/app.py:548-549`); if binding raises an `HTTPException`, it is stored as `request.routing_exception` (`src/flask/ctx.py:328-329`);
- initializes `_cv_token = None` and `_push_count = 0` (`src/flask/ctx.py:331-334`).

Nothing is proxy-visible yet: the module-level proxies resolve through the `_cv_app` ContextVar (`src/flask/globals.py:40`), which is still unset.

**Context push.** `ctx.push()` (`src/flask/app.py:1596` → `src/flask/ctx.py:416`) increments `_push_count` (`src/flask/ctx.py:428`), then on the first push:
1. `_cv_token = _cv_app.set(self)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:433`) — this makes the context active, so `app_ctx`, `current_app`, `g`, and `request` proxies resolve (`src/flask/globals.py:41-58`);
2. sends `appcontext_pushed` (`src/flask/ctx.py:434`);
3. because this context has a request, opens the session: `self._get_session()` → `session_interface.open_session(app, request)`, falling back to `make_null_session` if it returns `None` (`src/flask/ctx.py:439`, `381-392`; default interface `SecureCookieSessionInterface`, `src/flask/app.py:252`); the `session` proxy is now backed by a real object;
4. performs URL matching: `match_request()` → `url_adapter.match(return_rule=True)`, storing `url_rule`/`view_args` on success or `routing_exception` on `HTTPException` (`src/flask/ctx.py:444`, `405-413`). Only now do `request.url_rule`, `request.view_args`, `request.endpoint`, and `request.blueprints` become meaningful (`src/flask/wrappers.py:43`, `47`, `147-157`, `181`).

(Note: the class docstring at `src/flask/ctx.py:295-296` claims the session is loaded lazily on first access, but the code opens it eagerly inside `push()` at `src/flask/ctx.py:439`; the `session` property only additionally marks `accessed = True` at `src/flask/ctx.py:402`. The test at `tests/test_session_interface.py:16-32` confirms `open_session` runs before matching, since it may call `match_request()` itself.)

**Request dispatch.** `response = self.full_dispatch_request(ctx)` (`src/flask/app.py:1597`). `full_dispatch_request` (`src/flask/app.py:992`) marks `_got_first_request = True` (`src/flask/app.py:1010`), sends `request_started` (`src/flask/app.py:1013`), runs `preprocess_request` (URL-value preprocessors, then `before_request` functions, either of which can short-circuit dispatch; `src/flask/app.py:1014`, `1366-1391`), then `dispatch_request` (`src/flask/app.py:1016`). `dispatch_request` (`src/flask/app.py:966`) re-raises any stored routing exception via `raise_routing_exception` (`src/flask/app.py:978-979`, `562-584`), answers automatic `OPTIONS`, and otherwise calls the view: `self.ensure_sync(self.view_functions[rule.endpoint])(**view_args)` (`src/flask/app.py:990`). Exceptions go to `handle_user_exception` (`src/flask/app.py:1018`, `865`) and, if unhandled, to `handle_exception` (`src/flask/app.py:897`), which sends `got_request_exception` (`src/flask/app.py:926`), may re-raise (propagation), and otherwise finalizes a 500.

**Response finalization.** `finalize_request` (`src/flask/app.py:1021`) converts the return value with `make_response` (`src/flask/app.py:1037`), runs `process_response` (`src/flask/app.py:1039` → `1394-1418`): first `after_this_request` functions from `ctx._after_request_functions` (`src/flask/app.py:1407`), then `after_request` functions in reverse registration order (`src/flask/app.py:1411-1412`), then `save_session` unless the session is null (`src/flask/app.py:1416`). It then sends `request_finished` with the response (`src/flask/app.py:1042-1044`). Back in `wsgi_app`, the WSGI response is returned via `response(environ, start_response)` (`src/flask/app.py:1604`).

**Context pop.** The `finally` block (`src/flask/app.py:1605`) optionally hands the context to the debug/test preserve mechanism (`src/flask/app.py:1606-1607`), optionally clears `error` via the deprecated `should_ignore_error` (`src/flask/app.py:1609-1614`), and always calls `ctx.pop(error)` (`src/flask/app.py:1616`). `pop` (`src/flask/ctx.py:446`) validates the context is the active one, and on the final pop runs, each guarded by `_CollectErrors` (`src/flask/helpers.py:654-682`, so every callback runs even if one raises, with errors raised as a group at `src/flask/ctx.py:503`): `do_teardown_request(self, exc)` (teardown_request functions plus `request_tearing_down`, `src/flask/ctx.py:488-490`; `src/flask/app.py:1420-1450`), `request.close()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:491-493`), `do_teardown_appcontext(self, exc)` (teardown_appcontext functions plus `appcontext_tearing_down`, `src/flask/ctx.py:495-496`; `src/flask/app.py:1453-1479`), then deactivates the context (`_cv_app.reset`, `_cv_token = None`, `src/flask/ctx.py:498-499`) and sends `appcontext_popped` (`src/flask/ctx.py:501-502`).

## 1. Which context object, and what becomes available when

A single `AppContext` created with request data (`src/flask/ctx.py:260`, `340-348`) — since 3.2 there is no separate request context; `RequestContext` is a deprecated alias (`src/flask/ctx.py:528-540`). It is made active by `_cv_app.set(self)` in `push()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:433`).

| Stage | Newly available |
|---|---|
| Creation (`app.py:1592` → `ctx.py:300-334`) | `ctx.request` (a `Request`), `ctx.g`, `ctx.url_adapter` exist on the context object; no proxies work yet |
| Push, after `_cv_app.set` (`ctx.py:433`) | `app_ctx`, `current_app`, `g`, `request` proxies resolve (`globals.py:40-58`) |
| Push, after session open (`ctx.py:439`) | `session` proxy backed by a real session |
| Push, after `match_request` (`ctx.py:444`) | `request.url_rule`, `request.view_args`, and derived `request.endpoint`, `request.blueprints` (`wrappers.py:43-181`) |
| Dispatch (`app.py:1013-1018`) | `before_request` hooks, then the view; `request_started` receivers already fired |
| Finalization (`app.py:1037-1044`) | `after_request` hooks run; session saved; `request_finished` carries the response |
| Pop (`ctx.py:488-502`) | teardown callbacks receive the context's data; after `_cv_app.reset` nothing proxy-visible remains |

## 2. Actual order of the five operations

1. **App-context push signaling** — `appcontext_pushed.send` in `push()`, `src/flask/ctx.py:434`.
2. **Session opening** — `_get_session()` in `push()`, `src/flask/ctx.py:439` (deliberately before matching so custom URL converters can use the session; comment at `src/flask/ctx.py:440-442`).
3. **URL matching** — `match_request()` in `push()`, `src/flask/ctx.py:444`.
4. **Request-start signaling** — `request_started.send` at the top of `full_dispatch_request`, `src/flask/app.py:1013`, i.e. after push has fully completed.
5. **Request-finished signaling** — `request_finished.send` in `finalize_request` after `process_response` (which itself saves the session), `src/flask/app.py:1039-1044`.

So: `appcontext_pushed` → session open → URL match → `request_started` → view/before/after hooks → `request_finished`.

## 3. Repeated pushes and the exception hand-off

**Repeated pushes.** `push()` increments `_push_count` (`src/flask/ctx.py:428`); if `_cv_token is not None` it returns immediately (`src/flask/ctx.py:430-431`). So a second push changes only the counter: no second `appcontext_pushed`, no session re-open (the already-loaded `_session` is kept), and no re-match. Symmetrically, `pop()` decrements the counter and returns early while it is still above zero (`src/flask/ctx.py:481-483`), so the context stays active and no teardown runs until it has been popped as many times as it was pushed (docstrings at `src/flask/ctx.py:425-427` and `457-460`). This nesting is what lets `stream_with_context` re-push the current context inside the response generator via `with ctx:` (`src/flask/helpers.py:130`) so `request`/`session`/`g` survive after the request ends, and what lets the test client preserve and re-push contexts (`src/flask/app.py:1606-1607`; `src/flask/testing.py:188-189`, `246-248`).

**Exception into cleanup.** The responsible operation is `ctx.pop(error)` in `wsgi_app`'s `finally` block (`src/flask/app.py:1616`), where `error` was captured by `except Exception as e: error = e` (`src/flask/app.py:1598-1600`) or the bare `except:` for non-`Exception` failures (`src/flask/app.py:1601-1603`). `pop(exc)` forwards that exception into `do_teardown_request(self, exc)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:490`) and `do_teardown_appcontext(self, exc)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:496`), which pass it to every teardown function and to the `request_tearing_down`/`appcontext_tearing_down` signals (`src/flask/app.py:1449`, `1477`). The `with`-block equivalent is `AppContext.__exit__` → `self.pop(exc_value)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:516`). If an error handler handled the exception, `error` stays `None` and teardown receives `None` — matching the tests at `tests/test_reqctx.py:22-52`.

## Confidence

| Subquestion | Confidence | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Context object and per-stage availability | High | Direct read of `ctx.py` creation/push/pop, `globals.py` proxies, `wrappers.py` attributes; single code path, no ambiguity |
| 2. Order of the five operations | High | Line-sequenced within `push()` (`ctx.py:433-444`) and `full_dispatch_request`/`finalize_request` (`app.py:1013`, `1042`); corroborated by `tests/test_session_interface.py` |
| 3. Multi-push behavior and exception hand-off | High | `_push_count` logic at `ctx.py:428-431`/`481-483`; `ctx.pop(error)` at `app.py:1616` with `exc` forwarded at `ctx.py:490/496`; one caveat: the `ctx.py:295-296` docstring contradicts the eager session-open code, but the code and tests are unambiguous |

I've gathered all the evidence. Here is the complete teardown trace for this Flask 3.2.0.dev codebase.

# Outcome

Teardown for both a successful and a failed request runs through one code path, `AppContext.pop`, in this exact order: blueprint `teardown_request` callbacks (innermost blueprint → ancestors → app), `request_tearing_down` signal, `request.close()`, app `teardown_appcontext` callbacks, `appcontext_tearing_down` signal, context-variable reset, `appcontext_popped` signal, then a final aggregated error raise. Registration order matters within each scope (LIFO) and across scopes (blueprints before app), and since Flask 3.2 every teardown callback runs even if earlier ones raise, with errors collected into nested exception groups.

---

## 1. Exact teardown ordering

Both a successful request and a request with an unhandled exception follow the **identical** sequence. `wsgi_app` records the error and pops the context in a `finally` block, so teardown always runs; only the `exc` value passed to callbacks differs (`src/flask/app.py:1592-1616`).

Within `AppContext.pop` (`src/flask/ctx.py:446-504`):

1. **Blueprint `teardown_request` callbacks** — iterated as `chain(ctx.request.blueprints, (None,))`: innermost (child) blueprint first, then each ancestor, then app-level `None` last; within each scope, `reversed()` registration order (`src/flask/app.py:1442-1446`)
2. **`request_tearing_down` signal** — sent with `exc` kwarg (`src/flask/app.py:1448-1449`); any errors from steps 1-2 raise as `ExceptionGroup("Errors during request teardown")` at `src/flask/app.py:1451`, caught by `pop`'s collector
3. **Request closing** — `self._request.close()`, freeing request resources (`src/flask/ctx.py:492-493`)
4. **App `teardown_appcontext` callbacks** — `reversed()` registration order (`src/flask/app.py:1472-1474`)
5. **`appcontext_tearing_down` signal** — with `exc` kwarg (`src/flask/app.py:1476-1477`); errors raise as `ExceptionGroup("Errors during app teardown")` (`src/flask/app.py:1479`), again caught by `pop`
6. **Context-variable reset** — `_cv_app.reset(self._cv_token)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:498-499`); from here `current_app`, `g`, `request`, `session` proxies are unbound (`src/flask/globals.py:33-52`)
7. **`appcontext_popped` signal** — sent after the reset, so its receivers run with no active context (`src/flask/ctx.py:501-502`)
8. **Final error raise** — `collect_errors.raise_any("Errors during context teardown")` (`src/flask/ctx.py:504`)

Before all this: the response is returned to the WSGI server (`src/flask/app.py:1603`, `docs/lifecycle.rst:152`), and for unhandled errors `got_request_exception` was already sent during dispatch (`src/flask/app.py:926`). The docs list the same order at `docs/lifecycle.rst:153-159` and `docs/appcontext.rst:155-160`. Note steps 1-5 run while the context is still active (proxies usable inside callbacks); only `appcontext_popped` receivers run outside it. A test asserts the request-then-app sequence: `called == ["request", "app"]` (`tests/test_appctx.py:172-189`).

**Successful vs. unhandled exception:** ordering is unchanged. On success `error` stays `None` and `ctx.pop(None)` is called (`src/flask/app.py:1593`, `1616`). On an unhandled error, `error = e`, a 500 is produced by `handle_exception`, and `ctx.pop(e)` passes the exception to every callback and both signals.

## 2. Effect of registration order, including nested blueprints

**Within one scope: LIFO.** Callbacks append to a list at registration (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:538` for `teardown_request`; `src/flask/sansio/app.py:851` for `teardown_appcontext`) and execute via `reversed(...)` (`src/flask/app.py:1444`, `1472`). Last registered runs first.

**Across scopes: blueprints before app.** `request.blueprints` expands a matched nested name to `[full_dotted_name, parent, ...]` — e.g. `"parent.child"` yields `["parent.child", "parent"]` (`src/flask/wrappers.py:181-195`, `_split_blueprint_path` at `src/flask/helpers.py:645-651`). Chained with `None` last, a nested-child request runs teardown as: **child callbacks → parent callbacks → app callbacks**, each internally LIFO (`src/flask/app.py:1442-1446`).

**How nested names get there:** nested blueprints are registered under dotted names — `name = f"{name_prefix}.{self_name}".lstrip(".")` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:304`), with recursion into children at `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:376-377`. At registration, `_merge_blueprint_funcs` copies the blueprint's `teardown_request_funcs` into the app under the dotted key (`None` → `name`, non-`None` → `f"{name}.{key}"`), specifically for teardown at `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:380-385` and `404-406`.

This makes teardown the exact mirror of setup: `before_request` uses `names = (None, *reversed(req.blueprints))` — app, parent, child (`src/flask/app.py:1377`). `test_nested_callback_order` verifies it end-to-end: before-callbacks append `app_1, app_2, parent_1, parent_2, child_1, child_2`, and each teardown callback asserts `flask.g.seen.pop()` returns its own value, which only passes if teardown unwinds child → parent → app in reverse registration order (`tests/test_blueprints.py:914-994`).

Two more registration-order details:
- `Blueprint.teardown_app_request` registers on the app-level `None` key via `record_once` at first registration of the blueprint object (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:634-641`), so it runs among app-level callbacks, ordered by when the blueprint was registered, and runs for every request.
- If URL matching fails, `request.blueprints` is empty (docstring at `src/flask/wrappers.py:186-189`), so only app-level callbacks run.
- `teardown_appcontext` has no blueprint scoping at all — one flat app list, reverse registration order (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:360`, `851`).

## 3. Raising callbacks/receivers, and the `exc` value

The only difference is the `exc` argument: `None` for success, the original exception for unhandled errors (`src/flask/app.py:1593, 1598-1602, 1616`).

The full sequence inside `AppContext.pop(exc)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:446-504`):

1. **Blueprint request teardown callbacks**, innermost blueprint first, then each ancestor, each in LIFO registration order — `for name in chain(ctx.request.blueprints, (None,))` with `reversed(...)` at `src/flask/app.py:1442-1447`
2. **App request teardown callbacks** (the `None` key in the same loop, `src/flask/app.py:1442-1447`) — so app callbacks run after all blueprint callbacks
3. **Request teardown signal** `request_tearing_down` — `src/flask/app.py:1449`, sent only after all request teardown callbacks finish
4. `collect_errors.raise_any("Errors during request teardown")` — `src/flask/app.py:1451` (raises only if steps 1-3 errored; caught by `pop`'s outer collector)
5. **Request closing**: `self._request.close()` — `src/flask/ctx.py:493` (closes form-data file handles; werkzeug `Request.close`, `werkzeug/wrappers/request.py:301-310`)
6. **App-context teardown callbacks**, LIFO — `reversed(self.teardown_appcontext_funcs)` at `src/flask/app.py:1472`
7. **App-context teardown signal** `appcontext_tearing_down` — `src/flask/app.py:1477`, after all app-context callbacks
8. `collect_errors.raise_any("Errors during app teardown")` — `src/flask/app.py:1479`
9. **Context-variable reset**: `_cv_app.reset(self._cv_token)`, `_cv_token = None` — `src/flask/ctx.py:498-499` (after all app-context teardown, so teardown code can still use `current_app`/`g`)
10. **Popped signal** `appcontext_popped` — `src/flask/ctx.py:502`, sent after the contextvar is reset (receivers cannot rely on `current_app`)
11. `collect_errors.raise_any("Errors during context teardown")` — `src/flask/ctx.py:504`, the final combined raise for errors from steps 3-10

Notes:
- This runs only when the push count reaches zero: nested pushes of the same context are refcounted (`src/flask/ctx.py:481-484`).
- For a **successful request**: response is returned at `src/flask/app.py:1605` with `error = None` (`src/flask/app.py:1593`), so every callback and signal receiver receives `exc=None`.

So the last-registered callback runs first within its scope. Verified by `tests/test_basic.py:869-886`: with `before1, before2, after1, after2, finish1, finish2` registered, the recorded order is `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` — `finish2` (registered last) runs as step 5, `finish1` as step 6.

- `request.blueprints` returns names from **innermost to outermost** (`src/flask/wrappers.py:181-195`, via `_split_blueprint_path` at `src/flask/helpers.py:645-651`, which recursively strips `name.rpartition(".")[0]`). For a view in blueprint `parent.child`, the list is `["parent.child", "parent"]`, then `None` (app) is appended by the `chain`.
- So teardown order is: innermost blueprint's callbacks → parent blueprints' callbacks → app callbacks, regardless of when each was registered. This is the exact reverse of `before_request`, which iterates `(None, *reversed(req.blueprints))` — app first, then outermost to innermost (`src/flask/app.py:1377`).

Blinker's receiver call order is explicitly undefined (`blinker/base.py:220-221`), so ordering among signal receivers is not guaranteed. A failing `appcontext_popped` receiver is caught by the outer collector and included in the final group (`src/flask/ctx.py:501-504`).

Caveats: cleanup runs only when the outermost push is popped (`_push_count`, `src/flask/ctx.py:481-483, 332-337`); a plain app context (CLI command) has no request data, so steps 1-4 are skipped (`src/flask/ctx.py:488`); and preserved contexts (debugger/test client, `src/flask/app.py:1606-1607`, `src/flask/testing.py:188-189`) mean teardown may run again later (`src/flask/ctx.py:273-279`).

## 2. Effect of registration order

- **Within any bucket, execution is LIFO.** Registrations append (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:538` for `teardown_request`, `src/flask/sansio/app.py:851` for `teardown_appcontext`), and execution iterates `reversed(...)` (`src/flask/app.py:1444, 1472`). So the last-registered callback runs first. `tests/test_basic.py:858-897` shows `before` order 1,2 vs `teardown` order 2,1.
- **Blueprint vs. app callbacks are kept in separate dict keys.** `teardown_request_funcs` maps `scope → [funcs]` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:155-172`). App-level callbacks use key `None`; a blueprint's own `@bp.teardown_request` starts under the blueprint's local `None` key and is re-keyed at registration time to the blueprint's *registered (dotted)* name by `_merge_blueprint_funcs` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:379-407`, keying at `blueprints.py:385`). They therefore run only for requests whose endpoint belongs to that blueprint.
- **Nested blueprint names.** A nested child registered via `parent.register_blueprint(child)` gets `name = f"{name_prefix}.{self_name}"` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:302-304, 376`), producing endpoints like `parent.child.a`. `request.blueprint` is the endpoint minus the last segment (`src/flask/wrappers.py:170-177`), and `request.blueprints` splits the dotted name innermost-first: `_split_blueprint_path("parent.child")` returns `["parent.child", "parent"]` (`src/flask/wrappers.py:181-195`, `src/flask/helpers.py:644-651`). Since `do_teardown_request` iterates `chain(ctx.request.blueprints, (None,))` (`src/flask/app.py:1441-1442`), teardown order is child callbacks → parent callbacks → app callbacks — the exact reverse of `before_request` order, which iterates `(None, *reversed(req.blueprints))` (`src/flask/app.py:1377`). `tests/test_blueprints.py:909-993` verifies this with teardown functions popping `child_2, child_1, parent_2, parent_1, app_2, app_1` off `flask.g.seen`.
- **Name-based nuances.** `request.blueprint` reflects the registered name, which may differ from the creation name (`src/flask/wrappers.py:165-170` docstring). Because `_merge_blueprint_funcs` runs when `first_bp_registration or first_name_registration` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:316-331`), registering the same blueprint object again under a different `name=` copies its teardown functions under the new dotted key too; each copy fires only for requests matching that name. `Blueprint.teardown_app_request` instead registers into the app's `None` bucket via `record_once`, so it runs for every request, LIFO-interleaved with other app-level registrations made before it (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:634-641`).
- **App-context teardown has no blueprint dimension.** `teardown_appcontext_funcs` is a flat app-wide list (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:360, 824-851`); blueprints offer no app-context teardown decorator. Registration order matters only through the single `reversed()` at `src/flask/app.py:1472`.

## 3. Multiple exceptions, and the `exc` value

- **Every callback still runs.** Since 3.2 (`CHANGES.rst:17`, versionchanged notes at `src/flask/app.py:1434-1435, 1465-1466`), each callback call is wrapped in `with collect_errors:` (`src/flask/app.py:1445, 1473`), a `_CollectErrors` context manager that records the exception in `self.errors` and suppresses it by returning `True` from `__exit__` (`src/flask/helpers.py:654-675`). So one raising callback does not stop the remaining callbacks or the signal send.
- **Errors are grouped per phase, then combined.** `do_teardown_request` ends with `raise_any("Errors during request teardown")` (`src/flask/app.py:1451`) and `do_teardown_appcontext` with `raise_any("Errors during app teardown")` (`src/flask/app.py:1479`). Each phase group is itself caught by the pop-level collector in `AppContext.pop` (`src/flask/ctx.py:486-503`), so `request.close()`, the appcontext callbacks, the contextvar reset, and `appcontext_popped` still run. The pop-level `raise_any("Errors during context teardown")` at `src/flask/ctx.py:504` fires last. On Python ≥ 3.11 each `raise_any` raises `BaseExceptionGroup(message, errors)`; on older Pythons it re-raises only the first collected error (`src/flask/helpers.py:676-682`). `tests/test_appctx.py:216-266` verifies: on 3.11+ the client call raises an outer group "context teardown" containing two sub-groups ("request teardown" and "app teardown", each holding the callback's `ValueError` and the signal receiver's `ValueError`); below 3.11 only the first error (`request_teardown`) surfaces — yet all four still executed (`count == 4`).
- **Signal receivers are the exception to "everything runs".** A single blinker `Signal.send` propagates the first receiver's exception immediately, so receivers later in that send do not run, and receiver order is undefined (sets) — installed blinker `base.py:204-253` (docstring lines 217-223: "If a receiver raises an exception, that exception will propagate up."; loop at `base.py:242`). However, each `.send()` is itself inside `with collect_errors:` (`src/flask/app.py:1447-1448, 1475-1476`, `src/flask/ctx.py:500-501`), so a failing signal never blocks the rest of teardown; it just becomes one more error in that phase's group.
- **`exc` value received by each callback:**
  - **Handled errors → `None`.** If an `errorhandler` (or an `HTTPException` converted to a response, `src/flask/app.py:875-862`) produces the response, the exception never escapes `full_dispatch_request`, `error` stays `None` (`src/flask/app.py:1593`), and every request teardown callback, `request_tearing_down` receiver, appcontext teardown callback, and `appcontext_tearing_down` receiver receives `exc=None`. (Both signals pass `exc=exc`; `appcontext_popped` passes no `exc`.)
  - **Unhandled errors → the original exception object, identical for all callbacks.** With no matching handler, `error = e` holds the original exception (`src/flask/app.py:1598-1599`) and `pop(error)` passes it to `do_teardown_request` and `do_teardown_appcontext` (`src/flask/ctx.py:488-496`). Callbacks receive the *original* exception, not the `InternalServerError` wrapper that `handle_exception` builds (`src/flask/app.py:939-945`) — `tests/test_basic.py:810-849` asserts `type(exc) is ZeroDivisionError` in both teardown callbacks while the client sees a 500, and both receive the same object. The same value flows to `request_tearing_down` (`src/flask/app.py:1449`) and `appcontext_tearing_down` (`src/flask/app.py:1477`). This also holds when `handle_exception` re-raises in debug/testing, and for non-`Exception` `BaseException`s caught by the bare `except:` (`src/flask/app.py:1601-1603`).
  - **Manually managed contexts** pass the `with` block's exiting exception value: `__exit__` calls `self.pop(exc_value)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:508-517`), so an exception swallowed *inside* the block yields `exc=None` (`tests/test_reqctx.py:20-50`).

## Confidence table

| Subquestion | Confidence | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Exact ordering of the 8 stages + traces | High | Direct code path `ctx.py:446-504`, `app.py:1441-1479`; corroborated by `docs/lifecycle.rst:153-159`, `docs/appcontext.rst:155-160` and tests. The only undocumented step (`request.close()` placement) is explicit at `ctx.py:492-493`. |
| 2. Registration order, nested blueprint names | High | Code at `app.py:1441-1444`, `blueprints.py:302-304, 379-407`, `helpers.py:644-651`, `wrappers.py:162-195`; behavior confirmed by `tests/test_blueprints.py:909-993` and `tests/test_basic.py:858-897`. |
| 3. Multiple exceptions + `exc` semantics | High | `_CollectErrors` at `helpers.py:654-683`; two-level grouping visible in `app.py:1441-1479` and `ctx.py:486-504`; verified by `tests/test_appctx.py:216-266` and `tests/test_basic.py:810-849`. Medium only on blinker internals (single-`send` receiver abort, undefined order), cited from the installed blinker `base.py:204-253` rather than this repo. |

# Teardown Cleanup Trace in Flask (this repo, Flask 3.2-dev, merged `AppContext`/`RequestContext`)

Note first: in this version there is one combined context class, `AppContext` (`src/flask/ctx.py:247`), and "request context" just means an `AppContext` carrying request data (`src/flask/ctx.py:271-275`). Teardown is driven by `AppContext.pop()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:446-504`), called from `Flask.wsgi_app`'s `finally:` block (`src/flask/app.py:1605-1616`). The same cleanup sequence runs for a successful request and an unhandled error; only the `exc` value passed to callbacks differs (`src/flask/app.py:1581-1583` guarantees teardowns run "even if an unhandled error occurs").

## 1. Exact ordering

`wsgi_app` returns the response to the WSGI server first (`src/flask/app.py:1604`), then `ctx.pop(error)` runs in `finally` (`src/flask/app.py:1616`). Inside `pop` (with `_push_count` reaching 0; nested pushes defer cleanup, `src/flask/ctx.py:473-476`), the order is:

1. **Blueprint teardown callbacks, then app request-teardown callbacks, then `request_tearing_down` signal** — all inside `do_teardown_request` (`src/flask/app.py:1440-1451`), wrapped in `pop`'s collector (`src/flask/ctx.py:489-490`). Iteration is `for name in chain(ctx.request.blueprints, (None,))` (`src/flask/app.py:1442`): each blueprint bucket innermost-name-first, then the app bucket (`None`). Within each bucket, `reversed(...)` = last-registered-first (`src/flask/app.py:1444`). The signal is sent with `exc=exc` (`src/flask/app.py:1449`).
2. **Request closing** — `self._request.close()` (`src/flask/ctx.py:493`).
3. **App-context teardown callbacks, then `appcontext_tearing_down` signal** — `do_teardown_appcontext` (`src/flask/ctx.py:496`; `src/flask/app.py:1470-1479`): callbacks in `reversed(self.teardown_appcontext_funcs)` (`src/flask/app.py:1472-1474`), then the signal with `exc=exc` (`src/flask/app.py:1477`).
4. **Context-variable reset** — `_cv_app.reset(self._cv_token)` (`src/flask/ctx.py:498`); `current_app`, `g`, `request`, `session` proxies stop working (the proxies read `_cv_app`, `src/flask/globals.py:1-6`). So `appcontext_popped` receivers run with *no* active context.
5. **Popped signal** — `appcontext_popped.send(self.app, ...)` with no `exc` argument (`src/flask/ctx.py:502`).
6. **Deferred error raise** — `collect_errors.raise_any("Errors during context teardown")` (`src/flask/ctx.py:504`).

This matches the documented lifecycle (`docs/lifecycle.rst:153-159`, `docs/appcontext.rst:158-167`).

**Successful request:** `wsgi_app`'s `error` stays `None` (`src/flask/app.py:1590-1604`), so every callback/signal receives `exc=None` (verified: `tests/test_reqctx.py:16-27`).

**Unhandled exception:** dispatch-time exceptions caught by `full_dispatch_request`'s `except Exception` go to `handle_user_exception` (`src/flask/app.py:1006-1008`); if an `errorhandler` handles them, nothing escapes and teardown still gets `None`. If unhandled, the exception escapes to `wsgi_app`'s `except Exception` (`src/flask/app.py:1598-1600`) → `handle_exception`, which sends `got_request_exception` (`src/flask/app.py:926`) and either re-raises (`PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS`, testing/debug; the bare `except:` at `src/flask/app.py:1601-1603` records and re-raises, `finally` still pops) or builds a 500 response. Either way `error` holds the original exception (`src/flask/app.py:1599`), and the cleanup sequence above runs with `exc` = that original exception object (verified: `tests/test_signals.py:160-175` with `app.testing = False` shows `appcontext_tearing_down` receiving the `ZeroDivisionError` even though a 500 was returned; `tests/test_appctx.py:116-131` shows the same object reaching both the request-context pop and the outer `with app.app_context()` block's pop, since `__exit__` passes the escaping exception to `pop`, `src/flask/ctx.py:510-516`). One carve-out: deprecated `should_ignore_error`, if it returns `True`, resets `error` to `None` before pop (`src/flask/app.py:1609-1614`).

## 2. Registration order and nested blueprint names

- **Reverse (LIFO) within each scope.** `teardown_request` appends to a list (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:538`) and `teardown_appcontext` appends (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:851`); execution iterates `reversed(...)` (`src/flask/app.py:1444`, `1472`). So last-registered runs first, mirror-imaging `before_request`, which runs app-first/forward: `(None, *reversed(req.blueprints))` (`src/flask/app.py:1377`).
- **Blueprints before app.** The `chain(blueprints, (None,))` order means blueprint-scoped teardowns all run before app-level ones — the exact reverse of setup order. `tests/test_blueprints.py:874-972` (`test_nested_callback_order`) locks this in: `before` order `app_1, app_2, parent_1, parent_2, child_1, child_2`, and each teardown pops from the end of `flask.g.seen` (child teardowns first, app last).
- **Nested blueprint names.** A nested registration stores callbacks under the dotted registered name: `name = f"{name_prefix}.{self_name}".lstrip(".")` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:304`, nested pass sets `name_prefix` at `:376`), and `_merge_blueprint_funcs` keys teardown funcs under that full dotted name (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:380-386`, `404-406`). At request time, `request.blueprints` expands the matched endpoint's blueprint path — e.g. `"parent.child"` → `["parent.child", "parent"]` via `_split_blueprint_path` (`src/flask/wrappers.py:181-195`; `src/flask/helpers.py:645-651`) — so the **most-specific (innermost) blueprint's teardowns run first**, then each ancestor's, then the app's. A blueprint registered twice under different names gets separate buckets; only the bucket matching the request's endpoint path runs. `Blueprint.teardown_app_request` registers on the app bucket (`teardown_request_funcs[None]`) instead (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:634-640`), so those run among app-level teardowns in registration order interleave.
- **App-context teardown is scope-free:** a flat list, reversed; there is no blueprint keying (`src/flask/app.py:1472`, list defined at `src/flask/sansio/app.py:360`).

## 3. Multiple exceptions, and the `exc` value seen by callbacks

- **All callbacks still run.** Since Flask 3.2, each callback call is wrapped in `with collect_errors:` and `_CollectErrors.__exit__` swallows the exception by appending it to a list and returning `True` (`src/flask/app.py:1445-1446`, `1473-1474`; `src/flask/helpers.py:654-675`; changelog note `src/flask/app.py:1433-1435`, `1465-1466`). So one failing teardown callback does not stop later teardown callbacks or the signals.
- **Signal receivers are the exception.** `request_tearing_down.send` / `appcontext_tearing_down.send` are each wrapped in a single `collect_errors` block (`src/flask/app.py:1448-1449`, `1476-1477`). Blinker's `Signal.send` iterates receivers and propagates the first receiver exception immediately, so receivers scheduled after the failing one for that same signal are skipped (blinker 1.9.0, `uv.lock:55-56`; `.../blinker/base.py:242-251` in the uv cache: "If a receiver raises an exception, that exception will propagate up"). The rest of the teardown sequence is unaffected.
- **How errors surface.** `do_teardown_request` raises its collected errors at its end (`"Errors during request teardown"`, `src/flask/app.py:1451`), and `do_teardown_appcontext` likewise (`"Errors during app teardown"`, `src/flask/app.py:1479`) — but both raises happen inside `pop`'s outer collector (`src/flask/ctx.py:489-496`), so `request.close()`, app teardown, the contextvar reset, and `appcontext_popped` still execute. `pop` then raises everything at once (`src/flask/ctx.py:504`): on Python ≥ 3.11 a nested `BaseExceptionGroup("Errors during context teardown", ...)` containing the two inner groups plus any `close()`/popped-signal errors; on older Pythons, only the first collected error (`src/flask/helpers.py:676-682`). `tests/test_appctx.py:216-266` (`test_robust_teardown`) verifies: four failing hooks (request teardown, request signal, app teardown, app signal) all execute (`count == 4`), and the raised group nests as 2 sub-groups of 2 errors each.
- **`exc` value per callback — handled vs unhandled:**
  - Successful request → `None`.
  - Exception handled by an `errorhandler` (or an `HTTPException` handled into a response, or a `try/except` in the view/with-block body) → `None`, because the exception never escapes `full_dispatch_request` (docstring: "If an `errorhandler` is registered, it will handle the exception and the teardown will not receive it", `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:524-526`; verified in `tests/test_appctx.py:93-113` → `[None, None]` and `tests/test_reqctx.py:47-62`).
  - Unhandled exception → every request-teardown callback, `request_tearing_down` receiver, app-context-teardown callback, and `appcontext_tearing_down` receiver receives the **same original exception object** (passed through as `func(exc)` / `exc=exc`, `src/flask/app.py:1446`, `1449`, `1474`, `1477`) — including in production mode where a 500 response was generated. Teardown errors raised by earlier callbacks do not change the `exc` later callbacks receive.

## Confidence table

| Subquestion | Confidence | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Exact ordering (blueprint → app → request signal → close → appctx callbacks → appctx signal → contextvar reset → popped signal → deferred raise; identical skeleton for success/error) | High | `src/flask/ctx.py:446-504`, `src/flask/app.py:1440-1479`, `1566-1616`; matches `docs/lifecycle.rst:153-159` and `tests/test_appctx.py:172-190` |
| 2. Registration order (reverse/LIFO; blueprints before app, innermost-first; dotted nested names; `teardown_app_request` at app level) | High | `src/flask/app.py:1442-1444`, `1472`; `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:538`; `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:304`, `376`, `380-406`, `634-640`; `src/flask/helpers.py:645-651`; `tests/test_blueprints.py:874-972` |
| 3a. Multiple teardown-callback errors: collected, all callbacks run, nested `BaseExceptionGroup` on 3.11+ | High | `src/flask/helpers.py:654-682`; `src/flask/app.py:1440-1479`; `src/flask/ctx.py:484-504`; `tests/test_appctx.py:216-266` |
| 3b. Signal-receiver errors abort that signal's remaining receivers (blinker `send` propagates) | Medium-High | blinker 1.9.0 source in uv cache (`base.py:242-251`); Flask wraps the whole `send` in one collector (`src/flask/app.py:1448-1449`) |

I have all the evidence needed. Here is the complete trace.

## 1. Initial configuration construction

**The constructor chain.** `Flask.__init__` accepts `instance_relative_config: bool = False` (`src/flask/app.py:310-320`) and forwards it to the sansio base class via `super().__init__(...)` (`src/flask/app.py:323-333`). That lands in `App.__init__` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:279-288`), which first calls `Scaffold.__init__` (import name, static/template folders, `root_path` via `get_root_path`) — the base constructor at `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:75-97` does no configuration work at all.

**Instance path resolution.** Back in `App.__init__`, if no `instance_path` was given it is auto-discovered (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:300-301`); a user-supplied path must be absolute or a `ValueError` is raised (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:302-306`). `auto_find_instance_path` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:507-518`) returns `<package_path>/instance` for uninstalled code, or `<prefix>/var/<name>-instance` for installed packages (`find_package`, `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:754-793`). The result is stored as `self.instance_path` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:311`).

**Config creation.** `self.config = self.make_config(instance_relative_config)` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:316`). `make_config` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:479-493`) does exactly three things:
1. Picks the root: `root_path = self.root_path`, and if `instance_relative` is true, `root_path = self.instance_path` instead (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:488-490`).
2. Seeds defaults: `defaults = dict(self.default_config)` — a mutable copy of the class-level `ImmutableDict` defined on `Flask` at `src/flask/app.py:206-237` (`DEBUG: None`, `TESTING: False`, `SECRET_KEY: None`, `PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME: timedelta(days=31)`, `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME: "session"`, `MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE: 500_000`, `MAX_COOKIE_SIZE: 4093`, `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME: "http"`, `PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS: True`, etc.).
3. Overrides DEBUG from the environment: `defaults["DEBUG"] = get_debug_flag()` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:492`), then constructs `self.config_class(root_path, defaults)` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:493`; `config_class = Config` at `src/flask/sansio/app.py:193`).

**Source of the initial `DEBUG` value.** `get_debug_flag()` (`src/flask/helpers.py:28-33`) reads the `FLASK_DEBUG` environment variable (`src/flask/helpers.py:32`) and returns `bool(val and val.lower() not in {"0", "false", "no"})` (`src/flask/helpers.py:33`). So although the class default is `"DEBUG": None` (`src/flask/app.py:208`), the app's config always starts with `DEBUG` as a boolean taken from the environment, defaulting to `False`. (The `debug` property merely proxies this key: `self.config["DEBUG"]`, `src/flask/sansio/app.py:547-562`.)

**Effect of `instance_relative_config`.** `Config.__init__` (`src/flask/config.py:94-100`) stores `self.root_path = root_path` and seeds the dict with the defaults (`super().__init__(defaults or {})`, `src/flask/config.py:99`). Relative filenames in `from_pyfile` and `from_file` are resolved against this root: `filename = os.path.join(self.root_path, filename)` (`src/flask/config.py:204`, `src/flask/config.py:290`). With `instance_relative_config=True`, that root becomes the instance path rather than the app root path (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:489-490`). Absolute filenames are unaffected, since `os.path.join` discards the first argument when the second is absolute.

## 2. Which update wins; which keys are ignored

**The winner rule.** Every loader ultimately writes through plain dict assignment — `self[key] = value` in `from_object` (`src/flask/config.py:254`), `from_mapping` (`src/flask/config.py:320`), and `from_prefixed_env` (`src/flask/config.py:169`, `:183`), with the other three delegating to these. There is no merge priority, no protection of existing values, and no rollback on failure. Therefore, for a shared uppercase key, **the last call in the sequence that provides the key wins**, exactly like repeated dict writes. A method that fails to load (missing file with `silent=True`, returning `False`) writes nothing. Direct writes such as `app.config["KEY"] = v` or `app.debug = v` participate in the same last-write-wins semantics.

**Per-method behavior:**
- `from_object` (`src/flask/config.py:218-254`): imports the string via `import_string` if given a string (`:248-249`), then copies only attributes where `key.isupper()` (`:253-254`). Lowercase attributes are silently ignored. A `dict` argument does not work (keys are not attributes, per the docstring at `:226-228`).
- `from_pyfile` (`src/flask/config.py:187-215`): resolves against `root_path` (`:204`), executes the file into a fresh module (`:205-209`), then delegates to `from_object` (`:214`) — inheriting the uppercase-only filter. Missing files raise unless `silent=True` with errno `ENOENT`/`EISDIR`/`ENOTDIR`, which returns `False` (`:210-212`).

This repo is the Flask source itself (v3.2.0.dev, per `pyproject.toml`), so the answer comes straight from the framework's own code: `src/flask/app.py`, `src/flask/sansio/app.py`, `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py`, and `src/flask/config.py`. The short version: the app starts from a class-level `default_config` dict (with `DEBUG` overwritten from the `FLASK_DEBUG` env var), `Config` is a plain `dict` subclass, every `from_*` loader writes keys imperatively in call order with no overwrite protection, so the **last call that touches a key wins**, and the constructor reads no external file at all.

## 1. Initial defaults, the `DEBUG` source, and `instance_relative_config`

**Construction chain:** `Flask.__init__` (src/flask/app.py:310) immediately delegates to `App.__init__` via `super().__init__(...)`, forwarding `instance_path` and `instance_relative_config` (src/flask/app.py:317-334). `App.__init__` first calls `Scaffold.__init__` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:295-307), which discovers `root_path` from the import name when not supplied (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:96-100). Back in `App.__init__`, `instance_path` is auto-found if not given (src/flask/sansio/app.py:300-301) and stored (src/flask/sansio/app.py:311), then the single line that creates config runs: `self.config = self.make_config(instance_relative_config)` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:316).

**Initial defaults** come from `Flask.default_config`, an `ImmutableDict` of 30 keys (src/flask/app.py:206-237): `DEBUG: None`, `TESTING: False`, `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS: None`, `SECRET_KEY: None`, `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS: None`, `PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME: timedelta(days=31)`, `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME: "session"`, `MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE: 500_000`, `MAX_COOKIE_SIZE: 4093`, `PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS: True`, etc. `make_config` copies it into a mutable dict: `defaults = dict(self.default_config)` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:491), then constructs the config object via `config_class` (which is `Config`, src/flask/sansio/app.py:193) at src/flask/sansio/app.py:493. `Config.__init__` seeds the dict with those defaults and stores the root path: `super().__init__(defaults or {})` / `self.root_path = root_path` (src/flask/config.py:99-100).

**Source of initial `DEBUG`:** the `None` placeholder in `default_config` (src/flask/app.py:208) never survives construction. `make_config` unconditionally overwrites it: `defaults["DEBUG"] = get_debug_flag()` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:492). `get_debug_flag()` reads `os.environ.get("FLASK_DEBUG")` and returns true only if it is set and not one of `"0"`, `"false"`, `"no"` (case-insensitive) (src/flask/helpers.py:28-33). So the initial `DEBUG` is a bool derived from the `FLASK_DEBUG` environment variable, defaulting to `False` when unset. The `app.debug` property just proxies this key (`return self.config["DEBUG"]`, src/flask/sansio/app.py:547-557).

**Effect of `instance_relative_config`:** it selects *which* path becomes the `Config` object's `root_path` (the base for relative filenames in `from_pyfile`/`from_file`). In `make_config` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:488-490):
- `False` (default): `root_path = self.root_path`, the application root.
- `True`: `root_path = self.instance_path` — the instance folder, auto-located as `<package_path>/instance` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:517) or `<prefix>/var/<name>-instance` for installed packages (src/flask/sansio/app.py:518), or an explicit absolute `instance_path` from the constructor (relative values are rejected, src/flask/sansio/app.py:302-307).

It changes only the config's file base; the app's `root_path` used for static/template files is untouched.

## 2. Which update wins, and which keys are ignored

`Config` subclasses `dict` (src/flask/config.py:50), so all loaders mutate one flat shared mapping. Every loader ends in an unconditional `self[key] = value` assignment. There is no first-write-wins protection, no precedence ordering between methods, and defaults are not protected. Therefore, for any sequence of calls, **the last call in the sequence that sets the key wins**; earlier writes (including the constructor defaults) are simply overwritten. How each call funnels into that assignment:

- **`from_object(obj)`** — imports the name if given a string (src/flask/config.py:248-249), then iterates `dir(obj)` and copies only attributes where `key.isupper()` (src/flask/config.py:252-254). So only uppercase attributes of a module/class are loaded; lowercase attributes are silently ignored. This is why a `dict` argument doesn't work (its keys aren't attributes).
- **`from_pyfile(filename)`** — joins the filename with `self.root_path` (src/flask/config.py:204), executes the file's contents in a fresh module namespace (`types.ModuleType("config")`, src/flask/config.py:203), and delegates to `from_object` (src/flask/config.py:215). Same rule: only uppercase names in the file are loaded.
- **`from_file(filename, load)`** — joins with `self.root_path` (src/flask/config.py:290), calls your `load` callable on the file handle, and delegates to `from_mapping` (src/flask/config.py:302).
- **`from_mapping(...)`** — merges the positional mapping and keyword args (src/flask/config.py:314-317), then sets only keys where `key.isupper()` (src/flask/config.py:318-320). Non-upper keys are silently dropped.
- **`from_envvar(variable_name)`** — reads the env var and delegates entirely to `from_pyfile` (src/flask/config.py:114-124); if the variable is unset it raises `RuntimeError` (or returns `False` with `silent=True`) without touching config.
- **`from_prefixed_env(prefix="FLASK")`** — sets `prefix = f"{prefix}_"` (src/flask/config.py:152), iterates `sorted(os.environ)` (src/flask/config.py:154), skips env vars not matching the prefix (src/flask/config.py:155-156), strips the prefix (src/flask/config.py:159), attempts `loads(value)` (JSON by default) and keeps the raw string if parsing fails (src/flask/config.py:161-165), then writes **directly**: `self[key] = value` (src/flask/config.py:169). Note this loader has *no* `isupper()` filter — the post-prefix key is used verbatim. Keys containing `__` are written into nested dicts (src/flask/config.py:172-183).

**Keys ignored, per method:**
- `from_object` / `from_pyfile`: non-uppercase attributes/names (src/flask/config.py:253). Test confirmation: a module defining `TEST_KEY`/`SECRET_KEY` loads them but `"TestConfig" not in app.config` (tests/test_config.py:6-9, 25-30).
- `from_file` / `from_mapping`: non-uppercase mapping keys (src/flask/config.py:319).
- `from_prefixed_env`: env vars not starting with `{prefix}_` (src/flask/config.py:155-156), e.g. `NOT_FLASK_OTHER` never appears (tests/test_config.py:48, 65-66); no case restriction applies to the resulting key.
- `from_envvar` / `from_pyfile` / `from_file` with `silent=True` on a missing file/variable: nothing is loaded, config left untouched (src/flask/config.py:114-121, 209-214, 296-300).

Within a single `from_prefixed_env` call, env vars are processed in `sorted()` order (src/flask/config.py:154); since distinct env keys map to distinct config keys (nested `__` keys write into sub-dicts rather than replacing the top key), this ordering does not normally create intra-call conflicts. Test confirmation of last-write-wins across loaders with typed env values: `FLASK_BOOL=true` yields `config["BOOL"] is True`, etc. (tests/test_config.py:48-66).

So for a shared uppercase key like `SECRET_KEY` or `DEBUG` touched by several loaders: initial value = default (or `FLASK_DEBUG`-derived value for `DEBUG`), then each subsequent call in program order overwrites it, and the final value is whatever the last call that mentioned the key wrote. Direct assignments (`app.config["KEY"] = ...` or `app.debug = True`, which writes `config["DEBUG"]` via `ConfigAttribute`, src/flask/config.py:43-48 and src/flask/sansio/app.py:559-561) participate in the same dict with the same last-write-wins rule.

## 3. Does Flask auto-load any external configuration file during construction?

No. No config file is read by the constructor; the only external input at construction time is the `FLASK_DEBUG` environment variable. The constructor path supports this:

1. `Flask.__init__` (src/flask/app.py:310) delegates up and then only sets up the CLI group and the static route (src/flask/app.py:335-370) — no `from_*` calls.
2. `App.__init__` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:279-316) computes `instance_path`, calls `make_config` (line 316), and initializes the aborter, JSON provider, `url_map`, blueprints/extensions dicts, and `_got_first_request` — no file I/O.
3. `make_config` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:479-493) only builds `defaults` from `dict(self.default_config)`, overrides `DEBUG` from the env var, and returns `self.config_class(root_path, defaults)` — a pure in-memory dict construction.
4. `Config.__init__` (src/flask/config.py:94-100) does `super().__init__(defaults or {})` and stores `root_path` — no reads.
5. `Scaffold.__init__` (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:74-100) sets `import_name`, static/template folders, and `root_path` — no config access.

Everything beyond those defaults requires explicit `from_*` calls by the application. Things that might look like exceptions are not part of construction: `.env`/`.flaskenv` loading via python-dotenv happens in `Flask.run()` (src/flask/app.py:632, 709-715, guarded by `FLASK_SKIP_DOTENV` via `get_load_dotenv`, src/flask/helpers.py:36-47) or in the `flask` CLI (src/flask/cli.py:698), and only ever sets *environment variables*, never config keys directly. The `flask run` CLI also re-reads `FLASK_DEBUG` there (src/flask/app.py:713-714). The `instance_relative_config` flag merely changes the base directory for *future relative* `from_pyfile`/`from_file` calls (src/flask/sansio/app.py:489-490); it does not itself load anything from the instance folder.

| 1a | Initial defaults | 30-key `Flask.default_config` `ImmutableDict` copied into `Config` at construction | High |
| 1b | Source of initial `DEBUG` | `FLASK_DEBUG` env var via `get_debug_flag()`, overwriting the `None` default; `False` when unset | High |
