- The app registers the parent with `name="v1"`, so the parent's registration name is `v1` (resolved at src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:302-304, stored via `BlueprintSetupState.name` at :79).
- The parent registers the child with `name="sub"` and `name_prefix` set to the parent's own registration name (`bp_options["name_prefix"] = name`, src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:376), so the child's dotted registration name becomes `v1.sub`.
- The state for the child's registration then prefixes its routes with `v1.sub`, and the leaf endpoint defaults to the view function name `show`.

The end-to-end result is the dot-chain from app to innermost blueprint plus the view name. `test_blueprint_renaming` asserts exactly this shape: registering `bp` at `/a` and `/b` (name `alt`) with a nested `bp2` (name `sub`) produces `bp.index`, `alt.index`, `bp.sub.index2`, `alt.sub.index2` (tests/test_blueprints.py:1109-1116). Because each component name may contain no dot (enforced at blueprint construction, src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:195-199, and for endpoints at :427-431), dotted endpoint names unambiguously encode the nesting chain, and `Request.blueprint`/`blueprints` split on dots to recover it (src/flask/wrappers.py:162-193, src/flask/helpers.py:645-651).

**Final URL defaults: `{"fmt": "json", "extra": 1}`.** Defaults merge from two sources, both per-registration:
- The `BlueprintSetupState` combines the blueprint's constructor `url_values_defaults` with the registration-time `url_defaults` option: `self.url_defaults = dict(self.blueprint.url_values_defaults); self.url_defaults.update(self.options.get("url_defaults", ()))` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:83-85).
- A per-route `defaults=` option in `add_url_rule` is merged on top of those at replay time: `defaults = dict(defaults, **options.pop("defaults"))` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:106-108), and the result is passed as the rule's `defaults` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:110-115), which `App.add_url_rule` forwards into the Werkzeug `Rule` via `**options` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:647, :612).

For the child route above, its own state carries `{"fmt": "json"}`; the parent's registration-time `url_defaults={"extra": 1}` applies to the *parent's* routes, not the child's, because each nested blueprint gets its own setup state built from its own `bp_options` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:349-377). Only `url_prefix`, `subdomain`, and `name_prefix` propagate down the chain. So `show` ends with `{"fmt": "json"}`; a route defined on `parent` would end with `{"extra": 1}`. (If the parent were also given a subdomain, the child would combine it as `child_sub + "." + parent_sub`, src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:357-362.) `test_blueprint_url_defaults` demonstrates per-registration defaults: registering the same blueprint twice with different names/prefixes/defaults yields different view arguments per registration (tests/test_blueprints.py:131-148).

**Same blueprint registered twice with different names.** Each registration replays all deferred functions with a distinct setup state, so one `@bp.route` can produce two rules, two endpoints, and two view-function entries. `test_blueprint_renaming` asserts both sets of URLs and endpoints work (tests/test_blueprints.py:1109-1116), and `test_blueprint_url_defaults` asserts different defaults per registration (tests/test_blueprints.py:142-148).

## 3. Deferred callbacks, repeated registration, and endpoint collisions

**Deferred callbacks.** Everything on a blueprint that touches the app is deferred via `record`/`record_once` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:224-244), not just routes: `record_once` wraps the callback so it only fires `if state.first_registration` (:239-241). The `*_app_*` family (`before_app_request`, `after_app_request`, `teardown_app_request`, `app_context_processor`, `app_errorhandler`, `app_url_defaults`, `app_url_value_preprocessor`, `add_app_template_filter/test/global`, src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:495, :553, :611, :618, :628, :638, :650, :667, :679, :689) all use `record_once`, so they attach to the app exactly once even if the blueprint is registered repeatedly. Plain `record` callbacks (routes, and per-blueprint request hooks) replay on *every* registration, each against that registration's `BlueprintSetupState`. Two flags computed in `register` control the one-time merges: `first_bp_registration = not any(bp is self ...)` (first time this object is attached at all) and `first_name_registration = name not in app.blueprints` (first time this dotted name is used), and `_merge_blueprint_funcs` (error handlers scoped by name, `view_functions` copied verbatim, and per-scope hook lists extended under prefixed keys) runs `if first_bp_registration or first_name_registration` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:316-332, merge logic at :379-407). There is no deferral on the app: `@app.route`, `@app.errorhandler`, etc. mutate `url_map`, `view_functions`, and the hook lists immediately, guarded only by the first-request lock.

**Repeated registration.** Registering the *same* blueprint object again is allowed as long as the dotted name differs; registering *any* blueprint under a name already present in `app.blueprints` raises `ValueError` with a message directing you to `name=` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:306-314). `test_unique_blueprint_names` pins all four cases: same bp + same name = error; same bp + new name = ok; different bp + same name = error; different bp + new name = ok (tests/test_blueprints.py:1066-1081). Two caveats follow from the code. First, after the first registration the blueprint's setup is locked (`_got_registered_once = True`, src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:320), so you cannot add routes to it between registrations; the *same* `deferred_functions` list is replayed for every subsequent registration (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:334-335). Second, `app.blueprints` is keyed by name and "does not track how often they were attached" (src/flask/sansio/app.py:368-374), so re-registering the same object under a second name overwrites nothing but adds a second entry. Direct app registration has no equivalent: `app.add_url_rule` cannot be "replayed," and adding a rule with the same rule string twice simply adds two Werkzeug rules (the map tolerates it), while the endpoint check below governs the view mapping.

**Endpoint collisions.** There are two distinct collision points. (1) *Registration-name collisions* are checked in `Blueprint.register` before anything is applied, so a duplicate name fails cleanly before any rules are added (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:306-314). (2) *View-function collisions* are caught inside `App.add_url_rule`: when `view_func is not None` and the endpoint already maps to a *different* function, it raises `AssertionError: "View function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint function: ..."` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:651-657). Registering the *identical* function object again is silently accepted (`old_func != view_func` is False), which is what lets the same blueprint be registered twice under different names without tripping this: the prefixed endpoints (`bp.index` vs `alt.index`) differ, so each registration gets its own endpoint (tests/test_blueprints.py:1109-1116). The blueprint path makes collisions *unlikely by construction* rather than differently handled: names may not contain dots (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:195-199), and endpoints/view names may not either (:427-431), so the only way two blueprint routes collide on an endpoint is registering two same-named blueprints, which step (1) already blocks. The app path has no such namespace: `@app.route("/x")` and `@app.route("/y")` on two same-named functions collide directly at the `view_functions` check. Notably, `Scaffold.endpoint` writes `self.view_functions[endpoint] = f` with no collision check on either object (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:436, :453-454); on a blueprint this dict is later copied into the app verbatim by `_merge_blueprint_funcs` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:399-400), so a blueprint `@bp.endpoint("bar")` can silently shadow an existing app view (this is exactly what tests/test_blueprints.py:336-353 relies on: the blueprint's `bar` endpoint is not routable at the app level because it was never wired to a rule, only to the function registry).

**Summary of the contrast.** Direct app registration is a single synchronous write to `url_map` + `view_functions` with a bare endpoint. Blueprint registration is a two-phase commit: a definition phase that records closures with their rule/endpoint/options, and a replay phase at `register_blueprint` time that binds each closure to a `BlueprintSetupState` carrying the effective prefix, dotted name, subdomain, and defaults for that particular registration. That state is why one blueprint can be mounted at several prefixes/names, each replay producing independent rules and endpoints, while per-app hooks fire only once and duplicate registration names are rejected up front.

---

## Confidence table

| # | Subquestion | Confidence | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Route decorator and URL-rule path in both cases; when a blueprint route becomes an app rule/mapping | High | Read `Scaffold.route`, `App.add_url_rule`, `Blueprint.add_url_rule`/`record`/`register`, and `BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule` in full; the replay loop at sansio/blueprints.py:334-335 is the unambiguous transition point |
| 2 | Derived final URL rule, endpoint, and defaults with prefix, custom name, nesting | High | Derivation follows directly from the prefix join (98-100, 367-374), the dotted endpoint format (112), and the defaults merge (83-85, 106-108); corroborated by test_blueprint_renaming (1109-1116), test_nesting_url_prefixes (1003-1021), and test_blueprint_url_defaults (131-148). Not executed at runtime (werkzeug not installed in this environment), but every step is line-cited |
| 3 | Deferred callbacks, repeated registration, endpoint collisions vs. direct registration | High | `record`/`record_once` semantics (224-244), first-registration flags (316-332), name collision check (306-314), `view_functions` overwrite check (app.py:651-657) all read directly; behavior confirmed against test_unique_blueprint_names (1066-1081) |

One nuance worth flagging from subquestion 2: the `extra: 1` default belongs to the parent's routes only; it does not propagate into the nested child's defaults because nested blueprints receive their own setup state, and only `url_prefix`, `subdomain`, and `name_prefix` are inherited down the chain (sansio/blueprints.py:349-377).

control.answer:
I have all the evidence I need. This codebase is **Flask** (the Pallets framework), and the question maps directly onto `Scaffold.route`/`add_url_rule`, `App.add_url_rule`, and `Blueprint.register`/`BlueprintSetupState`.

# 1. The two registration paths

## Direct app registration: immediate

`@app.route(rule)` and `Blueprint` share the *same* `route` decorator because both `Flask` and `Blueprint` inherit from `Scaffold`. The decorator pops an explicit `endpoint` option, calls `self.add_url_rule(rule, endpoint, f, **options)`, and returns `f` unchanged (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:336`, `360-363`).

For an app, `add_url_rule` is `App.add_url_rule` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:368` is the abstract; the implementation is `src/flask/sansio/app.py:602`). It runs synchronously at decoration time:

1. Derives the endpoint from `view_func.__name__` if not given (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:610`, via `_endpoint_from_view_func` at `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:701-705`).
2. Computes methods (default `("GET",)` plus `view_func.required_methods`, plus `OPTIONS` when `provide_automatic_options` is on) (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:614-644`).
3. Constructs a `werkzeug.routing.Rule` via `url_rule_class` and adds it to `self.url_map` immediately (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:647-650`; `url_rule_class = Rule` at `src/flask/sansio/app.py:254`, `url_map` created at `:402`).
4. Stores `view_functions[endpoint] = view_func`, raising `AssertionError` if a *different* function already claims that endpoint (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:651-658`).

So with direct app registration, **the URL rule is in `app.url_map` and the view-function mapping is in `app.view_functions` at the moment the decorator runs**. There is no deferral stage.

## Blueprint registration: deferred, applied at `register_blueprint` time

`Blueprint.add_url_rule` does not touch any map. It validates that `endpoint` and the view-function's `__name__` contain no dot (dots are reserved as the blueprint-name separator) (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:413-431`), then appends a closure to `self.deferred_functions` via `record` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:433-440`; `record` itself is `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:224-231`, the list initialized at `:204`).

**A blueprint route becomes a real application URL rule and view-function mapping exactly when `app.register_blueprint(bp)` is called.** `App.register_blueprint` just forwards to `Blueprint.register` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:567-592`, `blueprint.register(self, options)` at `:592`). `Blueprint.register` then:

- Builds a `BlueprintSetupState(app, options, first_registration)` via `make_setup_state` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:321`, `246-253`).
- Iterates `for deferred in self.deferred_functions: deferred(state)` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:334-335`).

Each recorded route closure calls `BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:87-116`), which does the prefix/prefix-name work (detailed in Q2) and finally calls **the same `App.add_url_rule`** the direct path used (`self.app.add_url_rule(...)` at `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:110-115`). From that point the rule is indistinguishable from an app-level rule: same `url_map`, same `view_functions` dict, same endpoint-collision check, same error.

The only guard on ordering is `setupmethod`/`_check_setup_finished`: a blueprint locks all setup methods after its first registration (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:42-51`; `Blueprint._check_setup_finished` raises at `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:213-222`), so you cannot add routes to a blueprint *after* registering it. For apps, the lock is the first request instead (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:410-420`).

# 2. Deriving the final rule, endpoint, and defaults

## The rule (URL prefix)

`BlueprintSetupState.__init__` resolves the effective prefix: the registration-time `url_prefix` option **overrides** the blueprint's constructor-level `url_prefix` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:72-77`). The same precedence holds for `subdomain` (`:66-71`) and the registration `name` (`:79`).

`BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule` then joins: if `rule` is non-empty, `rule = "/".join((self.url_prefix.rstrip("/"), rule.lstrip("/")))`; if empty, the prefix itself is the rule (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:98-101`). This collapses duplicate/leading/trailing slashes — parametrized in tests as `("/foo/", "//bar", "/foo/bar")` (`tests/test_blueprints.py:108-111`, test at `:120`).

## The endpoint (custom registration name)

The endpoint is built as `f"{self.name_prefix}.{self.name}.{endpoint}".lstrip(".")` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:112`), where:

- `self.name` = `options.get("name", blueprint.name)` — a `name=` passed to `register_blueprint` replaces the blueprint's own name for this registration (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:79`).
- `self.name_prefix` comes from nesting (below).
- the local `endpoint` defaults to the view function's `__name__` (`:104-105`).
- `.lstrip(".")` makes the expression correct when neither prefix nor custom name is in play.

Worked example from tests: `bp` registered with `url_prefix="/1"` gets endpoints `bp.foo`; registered again with `name="test2"` and `url_prefix="/2"` gets `test2.foo` (`tests/test_blueprints.py:142-149`); and `@bp.route("/bar", endpoint="bar")` yields endpoint `bp.bar` (`tests/test_blueprints.py:299-306`).

## The URL defaults

`BlueprintSetupState.url_defaults` starts as a copy of the blueprint's `url_values_defaults` (constructor arg), then is updated with the registration-time `url_defaults` option, so registration overrides constructor values (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:84-85`). Rule-level `defaults={"baz": 42}` then override *both*, via `defaults = dict(defaults, **options.pop("defaults"))` (`:106-108`). Precedence: **rule-level `defaults` > registration `url_defaults` > blueprint constructor `url_defaults`**. Confirmed by `tests/test_blueprints.py:131-149`: with registration `url_defaults={"bar": 23}` and route `defaults={"baz": 42}`, `/1/foo` returns `"23/42"`.

Additionally, `@bp.url_defaults` functions are merged per-scope into `app.url_default_functions` under the *dotted* blueprint name (`_merge_blueprint_funcs`, `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:379-415`, `extend` at `:381-388`), and at URL-build time `App.inject_url_defaults` walks the endpoint's blueprint path from root to leaf (`_split_blueprint_path` at `src/flask/helpers.py:645-651`; the chained walk at `src/flask/sansio/app.py:957-977`). Note these two mechanisms are distinct: constructor/registration `url_defaults` become werkzeug **rule defaults**, while `@bp.url_defaults` functions are **URL-build callbacks**.

## Nested blueprints

`parent.register_blueprint(child, ...)` just appends `(child, options)` to `parent._blueprints` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:256-271`, list at `:211`). Nesting only takes effect when the outermost blueprint is registered on the app: `Blueprint.register` computes the nested options and recurses (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:349-377`):

- `bp_options["name_prefix"] = name` — the parent's fully-resolved (possibly dotted) name becomes the child's name prefix (`:376`).
- URL prefixes concatenate: `state.url_prefix.rstrip("/") + "/" + bp_url_prefix.lstrip("/")`, where `bp_url_prefix` falls back to the child's constructor `url_prefix`; parent's prefix is inherited if the child has none (`:367-374`).
- Subdomains concatenate as `child + "." + parent` when both exist (`:359-365`).

So for `app.register_blueprint(parent, url_prefix="/parent")` with `parent.register_blueprint(child, url_prefix="/child")` and a route `@child.route("/")`, the final rule is `/parent/child/` and the endpoint is `parent.child.<view_name>` — verified by `tests/test_blueprints.py:902-908` (three-level case, `/parent/child/grandchild/`) and prefix-joining parametrization at `tests/test_blueprints.py:1005-1022` (all four combinations of constructor vs. registration prefixes produce `/parent/child/`). Renaming composes the same way: registering `bp` as `name="alt"` makes a nested `sub` blueprint's endpoints `alt.sub.<view>` (`tests/test_blueprints.py:1109-1116`).

# 3. Deferred callbacks, repeated registration, and collisions

## Deferred callbacks

Everything recorded on a blueprint is a `DeferredSetupFunction` appended to `deferred_functions` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:224-231`). Routes are re-applied on **every** registration by the `for deferred in self.deferred_functions: deferred(state)` loop (`:334-335`). Two registers of the same blueprint therefore produce two rule sets (this is how `bp` yields both `/1/...` and `/2/...` above).

`record_once` wraps the callback so it fires only when `state.first_registration` is true (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:233-244`). `first_registration` is computed in `register` as `first_bp_registration = not any(bp is self for bp in app.blueprints.values())` — i.e., true only the first time *this object* is registered on this app, regardless of name (`:316`). This is what powers the `app_*` variants: `before_app_request` (`:614-618`), `after_app_request`, `teardown_app_request`, `app_context_processor`, `app_errorhandler` (`:656-667`), `app_url_defaults`, `app_url_value_preprocessor`, and `add_app_template_filter`/`test`/`global` (`:495, :553, :611`) all use `record_once`, so app-scoped behavior is applied exactly once per app while blueprint-scoped routes are re-applied per registration.

`_merge_blueprint_funcs` is additionally gated by `if first_bp_registration or first_name_registration` (`:317-318`, call at `:331-332`): error handlers, view functions, and the before/after/teardown/context/url-default/url-value-preprocessor lists are copied into the app's structures under the dotted name (`:379-415`). This is what prevents blueprint-scoped `before_request` etc. from being duplicated when a blueprint is mounted twice under different names.

## Repeated registration

Same blueprint, same resolved name → `ValueError`: `if name in app.blueprints` raises "The name 'X' is already registered for {this|a different} blueprint" (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:306-313`). Note this is identity-aware in its message: `bp_desc = "this" if app.blueprints[name] is self else "a different"` (`:307`).

Same blueprint, different `name=` → allowed; routes re-run with the new prefix/name (`tests/test_blueprints.py:1071-1080`, and the two-mount test at `:142-149`).

Registering also permanently locks the blueprint: `self._got_registered_once = True` (`:320`) makes any later `setupmethod` call raise (`:213-222`). So you can register a blueprint many times, but you can never modify it after the first registration.

## Endpoint collisions

Two layers, both ultimately enforced in `App.add_url_rule`:

1. **Blueprint-level**: `name` collisions are caught up front in `register` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:306-313`). Endpoint strings with dots are rejected at declaration time (`:428-431`), because dots would make the blueprint-qualified name ambiguous.
2. **App-level**: `App.add_url_rule` raises `AssertionError("View function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint function: ...")` when a *different* function is already registered for the endpoint (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:652-656`). Re-registering the *same* function object is a no-op (`old_func != view_func` check at `:653`).

Crucially, **blueprint routes pass through this same check** because `BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule` calls `self.app.add_url_rule` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:110-115`). Since the endpoint is name-qualified (`bp.foo`, `alt.sub.index2`), a blueprint route cannot silently collide with an app route or a route from a differently-named blueprint — which is exactly why repeated registration *requires* a unique `name=`. The `test_endpoint_decorator` test shows the qualification also prevents blueprint and app rules from sharing endpoints: a blueprint `@bp.endpoint("bar")` coexists with an app rule for endpoint `bar` because the blueprint's copy is registered under `bp.bar`-qualified keys... rather, the test shows the blueprint's `foobar` view is reachable at its own prefixed rule while `/foo` still maps to the app's endpoint (`tests/test_blueprints.py:336-351`).

## Contrast with direct app registration

| Aspect | Direct app (`@app.route`) | Blueprint (`@bp.route` + `register_blueprint`) |
|---|---|---|
| When rule is live | Immediately at decoration (`sansio/app.py:647-658`) | Only when registered (`sansio/blueprints.py:334-335` → `:110-115`) |
| Endpoint | Bare view name (`sansio/app.py:610`) | `{name_prefix}.{registration name}.{endpoint}`, `.lstrip(".")` (`sansio/blueprints.py:112`) |
| Prefix | None | Registration `url_prefix` overrides constructor; nested prefixes join with `/` (`sansio/blueprints.py:72-77, 98-101, 367-374`) |
| Defaults | Rule-level only | Rule > registration > constructor layering (`sansio/blueprints.py:84-85, 106-108`) |
| Collision guard | One: `AssertionError` on different view for same endpoint (`sansio/app.py:652-656`) | Three: dotted endpoint rejected (`blueprints.py:428-431`), name uniqueness `ValueError` (`blueprints.py:306-313`), then same app-level `AssertionError` |
| Re-registration | N/A; `AssertionError` if the same endpoint gets a different view | Allowed with distinct `name=`; routes re-applied, app-scoped callbacks only once (`record_once`), blueprint funcs merged once per name (`blueprints.py:331`) |
| Lock | After first request (`sansio/app.py:410-420`) | After first registration, any setup method (`blueprints.py:213-222`) |
| Callbacks | Stored directly in app dicts (`scaffold.py:460-483, 584-594`) | Deferred; merged into app dicts under dotted names at registration (`blueprints.py:379-415`) |

---

## Confidence table

| # | Subquestion | Confidence | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Route decorator/URL-rule path in both cases; when a blueprint route becomes an app URL rule + view mapping | **High** | Read both `add_url_rule` implementations and the record/replay loop directly; every step cited with line numbers |
| 2a | Final URL rule derivation (prefix override + join + nesting) | **High** | Exact join expression at `blueprints.py:98-101, 367-374`; confirmed against 3 parametrized tests |
| 2b | Endpoint name with custom registration name and nesting | **High** | Format string at `blueprints.py:112` plus `:302-304, :376`; confirmed by `test_blueprint_renaming` (`alt.sub.index2`) |
| 2c | URL defaults precedence | **High** | `blueprints.py:84-85, 106-108`; confirmed by `test_blueprint_url_defaults` output `"23/42"` |
| 2d | Distinction between rule defaults and `@bp.url_defaults` build callbacks | **Medium-High** | Code is explicit (`_merge_blueprint_funcs` vs `url_defaults` state); behavior distinction inferred from `inject_url_defaults` walk, not runtime-tested here |
| 3a | Deferred callbacks: `record` vs `record_once`, `first_registration` semantics | **High** | `blueprints.py:224-244, 316, 334-335` plus all `app_*` users enumerated by grep |
| 3b | Repeated registration: name uniqueness `ValueError`, re-application of routes, `_got_registered_once` lock | **High** | `blueprints.py:306-320, 213-222`; matches `test_unique_blueprint_names` exactly |
| 3c | Endpoint collisions: three-layer guard, same shared `AssertionError` at app level | **High** | `blueprints.py:428-431, 306-313`; `sansio/app.py:652-656`; identity check `old_func != view_func` read directly |
| 3d | Contrast with direct app registration | **High** | Both code paths read in full; table derived line-by-line from cited sources |

The only place I'd flag residual uncertainty is 2d: the two defaults mechanisms are clearly separate in the code, but I did not execute a runtime check of their interaction, so that single row is slightly below the rest.

All three subquestions trace through the same machinery: blueprints register callbacks into their own scoped dictionaries, `Blueprint.register()` merges them into the app under dotted names, and at request time the app iterates scopes derived from the request's dotted blueprint name. Everything below uses this scenario:

- `app = Flask(...)`, `parent = Blueprint("parent")`, `child = Blueprint("child")`
- `parent.register_blueprint(child)`, `app.register_blueprint(parent)`
- Registered names become `parent` and `parent.child` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:304` builds `name = f"{name_prefix}.{self_name}".lstrip(".")`; the nested call passes `bp_options["name_prefix"] = name` at `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:376` then `blueprint.register(app, bp_options)` at `:377`), so a child route's endpoint is `parent.child.index` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:112`).

## 1. Blueprint-local vs app-wide registrations

**Local (blueprint-scoped) registrations.** `before_request`, `after_request`, `teardown_request`, and `errorhandler` are inherited from `Scaffold` and store the function on the blueprint's *own* dictionaries, under scope key `None`:

- `before_request` → `self.before_request_funcs.setdefault(None, []).append(f)` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:483`)
- `after_request` → `self.after_request_funcs.setdefault(None, []).append(f)` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:504`)
- `teardown_request` → `self.teardown_request_funcs.setdefault(None, []).append(f)` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:538`)
- `errorhandler` → `register_error_handler` → `self.error_handler_spec[None][code][exc_class] = f` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:653-654`), where `(exc_class, code)` comes from `_get_exc_class_and_code` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:657-698`: an int code maps to the default exception class for that code and keeps the code; an `HTTPException` subclass keeps its `.code` at `:696`; any other exception class gets `code=None` at `:698`).

Nothing is attached to the app yet. | Priority | Scope searched | Bucket |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | `parent.child`, then `parent`, then app (`None`) | code-specific bucket (`error_handler_spec[name][code]`) |
| 2nd | `parent.child`, then `parent`, then app (`None`) | class bucket (`error_handler_spec[name][None]`) |

- **Scope dominates class specificity within a bucket**: the name loop is outer, the MRO loop inner, so a superclass handler (e.g. a catch-all) registered on the child beats an exact-class handler registered on the parent or app.

The local decorators are inherited from `Scaffold` and store into the blueprint's own dicts under its local `None` key, pending registration:

| Registration | Storage on the blueprint | After `register_blueprint` | When it runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bp.before_request` | `self.before_request_funcs[None]` (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:483) | merged under the blueprint's dotted name (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:385, 402) | only requests dispatched to that blueprint's endpoints |
| `bp.after_request` | `self.after_request_funcs[None]` (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:504) | merged under dotted name (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:403) | only that blueprint's requests |
| `bp.teardown_request` | `self.teardown_request_funcs[None]` (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:538) | merged under dotted name (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:404-407) | only that blueprint's requests |
| `bp.errorhandler` / `bp.register_error_handler` | `self.error_handler_spec[None][code][exc_class]` (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:654) | merged under dotted name (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:388-397) | errors raised from that blueprint's views |

The `*_app_*` variants are deferred via `record_once` and append directly to the **application's** `None`-keyed (global) lists at registration time:

- `bp.before_app_request` → `s.app.before_request_funcs[None]` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:614-621)
- `bp.after_app_request` → `s.app.after_request_funcs[None]` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:624-631)
- `bp.teardown_app_request` → `s.app.teardown_request_funcs[None]` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:634-641)
- `bp.app_errorhandler` → `state.app.errorhandler(code)(f)`, i.e. the app's `error_handler_spec[None]` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:656-668, esp. 665)

So the two families are indistinguishable from `app.before_request`/`app.errorhandler` at runtime: they run for **every** request, not just the blueprint's. `record_once` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:233-244) fires only when `state.first_registration` is true, so app-wide callbacks register once per blueprint object even if it is mounted twice; the local merge is gated on `first_bp_registration or first_name_registration` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:332), so local callbacks are copied under each unique registered name. The docstrings state the equivalence explicitly ("Equivalent to :meth:`.Flask.before_request`", src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:616). Test confirmation: `errors.app_errorhandler(403)` catches aborts both on an app route and on another blueprint's route (tests/test_blueprints.py:78-101).

## 2. Callback order for a request handled by a nested blueprint

Take `app.register_blueprint(parent)` with `parent.register_blueprint(child)`, request to a `child` view. Endpoint is `parent.child.view`, so `request.blueprints == ["parent.child", "parent"]` (innermost first). Dispatch: `full_dispatch_request` (src/flask/app.py:992-1019) runs `preprocess_request` (1014), `dispatch_request` (1016), error handling (1018), then `finalize_request` (1019).

**Preprocessing** — `preprocess_request` (src/flask/app.py:1366-1392):

`names = (None, *reversed(req.blueprints))` (1377) = `(None, "parent", "parent.child")` — app first, outermost ancestor next, innermost blueprint last.

1. All `url_value_preprocessors` in that scope order (1379-1382)
2. All `before_request` funcs in the same scope order (1384-1391):
   - app `before_request` **plus any `before_app_request` callbacks** (they live in the same `None` list; they interleave in registration order)
   - `parent`-local `before_request` funcs (registration order)
   - `parent.child`-local `before_request` funcs (registration order)
3. The first callback returning non-`None` short-circuits everything after it and its value becomes the response (1389-1390, docstring 1370-1372)

Verified by tests/test_blueprints.py:914-991: the view at `/a` returns `"app_1, app_2, parent_1, parent_2, child_1, child_2"` (989-990).

**After processing** — `process_response` (src/flask/app.py:1394-1417):

1. `after_this_request` functions stored on the app context, in the order added (1407; appended at src/flask/ctx.py:147)
2. Then `for name in chain(ctx.request.blueprints, (None,))` (1410) — the **reverse** direction of preprocessing: `parent.child` first, then `parent`, then the app last. Within each scope, functions run in reverse registration order (`reversed(self.after_request_funcs[name])`, 1412):
   - `child`-local `after_request` (reverse registration order)
   - `parent`-local `after_request` (reversed)
   - app `after_request` **plus `after_app_request`** callbacks (the `None` list, reversed)
3. `save_session` (1416)

**Teardown** — `do_teardown_request` (src/flask/app.py:1420-1451), called from `AppContext.pop` (src/flask/ctx.py:490):

Same direction as after-processing: `chain(ctx.request.blueprints, (None,))` (1442), each scope's funcs in reverse registration order (1444), each receiving `exc` (1446):

1. `child`-local `teardown_request` (reversed, each passed `exc`)
2. `parent`-local `teardown_request` (reversed)
3. app `teardown_request` **plus `teardown_app_request`** (reversed)
4. `request_tearing_down` signal (1449)

Since Flask 3.2 all callbacks run even if one raises; errors are collected and raised as a group at the end of the phase (`_CollectErrors`, 1437-1451). The teardown test pops `g.seen` in exactly the reverse order of the before callbacks (tests/test_blueprints.py:920-921, 929-930, 937-938, 945-946). After request teardown: `request.close()` (src/flask/ctx.py:493), then `do_teardown_appcontext` (src/flask/ctx.py:496) runs `teardown_appcontext_funcs` in reverse order (src/flask/app.py:1472-1475) followed by the `appcontext_tearing_down` signal (1477), and finally `appcontext_popped` (src/flask/ctx.py:502). Note teardown funcs fire whether or not an error handler handled the exception; an *handled* exception never reaches teardown as `exc` (docstring, src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:516-519).

## 3. Error handler lookup order

`handle_http_exception` and `handle_user_exception` both call `self._find_error_handler(e, ctx.request.blueprints)` (src/flask/app.py:860, 890); unhandled non-HTTP exceptions go through `handle_exception`, which synthesizes an `InternalServerError` and looks up a handler for it (src/flask/app.py:897-947, esp. 943). Proxy exceptions without a code and internal `RoutingException`s are returned unchanged without handler lookup (src/flask/app.py:847-857).

`_find_error_handler` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:865-889) works in two phases:

1. `_get_exc_class_and_code(type(e))` yields `(exc_class, code)` — HTTPExceptions carry their code, other exceptions get `code=None` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:873; src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:695-698).
2. `names = (*blueprints, None)` (874) — **innermost blueprint first, then each ancestor, then the app**.
3. Phase loop `for c in (code, None) if code is not None else (None,)` (876):
   - **Phase 1 (code handlers):** for each scope innermost→ancestors→app, check `error_handler_spec[name][code]` (878) and walk `exc_class.__mro__` (883), most specific class first. First hit returns (885-887). Note that both `errorhandler(403)` and `errorhandler(Forbidden)` land in this code bucket, the former keyed by werkzeug's `Forbidden` class (registration: `error_handler_spec[None][code][exc_class] = f`, src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:654).
   - **Phase 2 (class handlers):** same scope order, but in the `None` code bucket, which holds handlers for non-HTTP exception classes (e.g. `ValueError`).
4. If nothing matches, `None` is returned and the exception propagates / is returned as the response.

So the precedence is: **innermost-blueprint code handler → ancestor code handlers → app code handler → innermost-blueprint class handler → ancestor class handlers → app class handler**, and within any single scope+bucket the most-derived registered class on the MRO wins. This matches the docstring order "blueprint handler for a specific code, app handler for a specific code, blueprint handler for an exception class, app handler for an exception class" (src/flask/sansio/app.py:869-872).

**How the dotted name supplies the scopes:** the matched endpoint's dotted prefix becomes `request.blueprint` (src/flask/wrappers.py:176), which is split into the ancestor chain `["parent.child", "parent"]` (src/flask/helpers.py:645-651). These strings are identical to the keys created at registration time by `_merge_blueprint_funcs` (dotted name from src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:304/376, rewrite at 385, storage at 397), which is why lookup finds nested-blueprint handlers at all. `None` (app scope) covers `Flask.errorhandler` and `app_errorhandler` registrations. Consequence: if routing itself fails (404/405), the endpoint is `None`, `blueprints` is `[]` (src/flask/wrappers.py:193), so only app-scope handlers are searched — the documented caveat that blueprint error handlers can't own a URL space (docs/blueprints.rst:275-287).

Test confirmation (tests/test_blueprints.py:865-912): `parent` and `grandchild` both register 403 handlers; an abort in `child`'s view resolves to the ancestor `"Parent no"` (910) because `child` has no handler and `parent`'s scope is searched before the app's; an abort in `grandchild` resolves to `"Grandchild no"` (912) because the innermost scope's code handler wins.

## Confidence table

| Subquestion | Confidence | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Local vs `*_app_*` registration semantics | High | Direct source of both registration paths (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:483/504/538/654 vs src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:614-668) plus behavior test (tests/test_blueprints.py:78-101) |
| 2. Preprocess / after / teardown order for nested blueprint, incl. app-wide | High | Order-defining loops read directly (src/flask/app.py:1377, 1410, 1442) and confirmed by dedicated order test (tests/test_blueprints.py:914-991) |
| 3. Handler lookup order and dotted-name scope derivation | High | `_find_error_handler` read directly (src/flask/sansio/app.py:865-889) with scope construction (wrappers.py:176/195, helpers.py:645-651) and nested-handler test (tests/test_blueprints.py:865-912) |

One nuance flagged with slightly less certainty: the claim that app-wide (`before_app_request`) callbacks interleave with `app.before_request` callbacks purely by registration order follows from both appending to the same list (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:619, src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:483), but no test pins the exact interleaving.

```python
exc_class, code = self._get_exc_class_and_code(type(e))   # :873
names = (*blueprints, None)                               # :874
for c in (code, None) if code is not None else (None,):    # :876
    for name in names:                                     # :877
        handler_map = self.error_handler_spec[name][c]     # :878
        for cls in exc_class.__mro__:                      # :883
            handler = handler_map.get(cls)                 # :884

```

1. **Code-specific handlers first, at every blueprint scope**: `parent.child.grandchild[403]` → `parent.child[403]` → `parent[403]` → app `[None][403]`
2. **Then class-based (code-`None`) handlers at every scope**, same order: `parent.child.grandchild[None]` → `parent.child[None]` → `parent[None]` → app `[None][None]`
3. Within each (scope, code) map: **MRO order** — a handler keyed by the concrete class (e.g. `Forbidden`) is found before one keyed by `HTTPException` or `Exception` (sansio/app.py:883-886). - **Code beats class across scopes**: an app-level `errorhandler(403)` is found before a grandchild-level `errorhandler(HTTPException)`, because the entire `c=403` pass finishes before the `c=None` pass starts (loop order at sansio/app.py:876-877).

# Default Signed-Cookie Session: Serialization & Deserialization Trace

**The stack:** `Flask` (default `session_interface = SecureCookieSessionInterface()`, `src/flask/app.py:252`) wraps `itsdangerous.URLSafeTimedSerializer` around Flask's own `TaggedJSONSerializer` (`src/flask/sessions.py:273, 313`). Session data → tagged JSON → base64 (+zlib) → HMAC-signed token in a cookie named `session` (`SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` default, `src/flask/app.py:218`).

---

## 1. Constructing the signing serializer

`get_signing_serializer` (`src/flask/sessions.py:303-321`) builds a fresh `URLSafeTimedSerializer` per call:

**Secret key (current).** `app.secret_key` proxies the `SECRET_KEY` config (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:213`), default `None` (`src/flask/app.py:211`). If falsy, **no serializer is built at all** — `open_session` returns `None` (`sessions.py:304-305, 325`) and the request context falls back to `make_null_session` → `NullSession` (`src/flask/ctx.py:388-391`), whose mutating methods raise `RuntimeError("The session is unavailable because no secret key was set...")` (`sessions.py:89-96`).

**Fallback keys.** If `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` is set (default `None`, `src/flask/app.py:212`), fallback keys are prepended to the key list, and the current key is appended **last**: `keys.extend(fallbacks)` then `keys.append(app.secret_key)` with the comment "itsdangerous expects current key at top" (`sessions.py:309-312`). This ordering matters: itsdangerous treats `secret_keys` as "oldest to newest" (`itsdangerous/signer.py:138-143`), **signs with the last (newest/current) key** (`signer.py:196`, `serializer.py:243`), and **verifies by iterating `reversed(secret_keys)`** — i.e., current key first, then fallbacks (`signer.py:236`). Result: new cookies are always signed with the current key; old cookies remain readable until fallbacks are removed. The fallback test confirms: after rotating to `"+1 key"` with fallbacks `["0 key", "-1 key"]`, the session still reads `{"a": 1}`, but with an unrelated key `"? key"` it reads `{}` (`tests/test_basic.py:393-418`).

**Salt.** `salt = "cookie-session"` (`sessions.py:291`) is passed as the serializer's `salt`, distinguishing session signatures from other uses of the same secret key. In itsdangerous, the salt feeds key derivation, not the signature input.

**Key derivation.** `key_derivation = "hmac"` (`sessions.py:296`), passed via `signer_kwargs` (`sessions.py:313-321`). For each key: `mac = hmac.new(secret_key, digestmod=sha1); mac.update(salt); return mac.digest()` (`itsdangerous/signer.py:206-208`). So the effective per-key signing key is `HMAC-SHA1(secret_key, msg="cookie-session")` — the salt is *signed into the derived key*, and this is the only place Flask differs from itsdangerous's own `django-concat` default (`signer.py:127`).

**Digest.** `digest_method = staticmethod(_lazy_sha1)` (`sessions.py:293`) where `_lazy_sha1` defers touching `hashlib.sha1` to runtime so FIPS builds can substitute something else before use (`sessions.py:276-282`). SHA-1 here is only the inner hash of the HMAC; its weakness doesn't directly apply.

**Tagged JSON serializer.** `serializer = session_json_serializer = TaggedJSONSerializer()` (`sessions.py:273, 300`), a module-level singleton. It's the *payload* serializer inside `URLSafeTimedSerializer` — itsdangerous handles signing/base64/compression, Flask handles JSON with extra types. The final token structure (from itsdangerous) is `payload + "." + base64(timestamp) + "." + base64(HMAC)` (sep default `"."`, `timed.py:50-51`).

---

## 2. Serialization into a cookie and restoration

**Write path** (`save_session`, `sessions.py:337-385`): the request context calls it after response generation unless the session is null (`src/flask/app.py:1415-1416`). If the session is empty: a modified-empty session deletes the cookie, an unmodified-empty one sets nothing (`sessions.py:358-368`). Otherwise, if `should_set_cookie` (`session.modified or (session.permanent and SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST)`, `sessions.py:233-246`) passes, it computes `expires` (`now + permanent_session_lifetime` **only if** `session.permanent`, else `None` — browser-session cookie; `sessions.py:225-230`) and does:

```python
val = self.get_signing_serializer(app).dumps(dict(session))   # sessions.py:373
```

then `response.set_cookie(name, val, ...)` with `HttpOnly` (default True), `SameSite`, `Secure`, `Partitioned`, `Domain`, `Path` from config (`sessions.py:374-381`). A `Vary: Cookie` header is added whenever the session was accessed (`sessions.py:349-350`).

**Payload serialization (dumps).** `dict(session)` → `TaggedJSONSerializer.dumps` → `dumps(self.tag(value), separators=(",", ":"))` — compact JSON (`src/flask/json/tag.py:321-323`). `tag()` walks the registered tag order and tags the first match (`tag.py:289-295`); dict/list values recurse via `PassDict`/`PassList` tagging each child (`tag.py:119-156`). itsdangerous then base64-URLsafe-encodes the JSON, zlib-compresses first if that's shorter (marked with a leading `"."`), and signs with `TimestampSigner`.

**Non-standard Python types.** Registered in `default_tags` (`tag.py:238-247`), each with a compact one/two-char key:

| Tag key | Class | Python → JSON | JSON → Python | Lines |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `" di"` | `TagDict` | 1-item dict whose key *is itself a tag key*; stores as `{key + "__": tagged}` | strips `__` suffix | `tag.py:93-116` |
| `" t"` | `TagTuple` | tuple → list of tagged items | `tuple(value)` | `tag.py:133-145` |
| `" b"` | `TagBytes` | `b64encode` → ASCII str | `b64decode` | `tag.py:159-169` |
| `" m"` | `TagMarkup` | `str(value.__html__())` | `Markup(value)` | `tag.py:173-188` |
| `" u"` | `TagUUID` | `value.hex` | `UUID(value)` | `tag.py:191-202` |
| `" d"` | `TagDateTime` | `http_date(value)` (RFC 822/1123 str) | `parse_date(value)` | `tag.py:205-215` |

Plain `dict` and `list` round-trip structurally via `PassDict`/`PassList` without emitting a tag key themselves (`tag.py:119-156`). `test_session_special_types` verifies all of these plus the collision-avoidance cases: storing literal `{" t": "not-a-tuple"}`, `{" t__": ...}`, `{" di": ...}` still round-trips correctly (`tests/test_basic.py:467-492`) — the `TagDict` `__`-suffix scheme means `{" t__": x}` is the *encoding* of a tuple-valued... rather, of a dict whose sole key is literally `" t"`, so user data containing tag-like keys survives.

**Read path** (`open_session`, `sessions.py:323-335`): get the serializer; if `None` → `None` (null session upstream). `val = request.cookies.get(self.get_cookie_name(app))` (`sessions.py:327`); empty/missing → fresh empty `SecureCookieSession()` (`sessions.py:328-329`). Otherwise:

```python
max_age = int(app.permanent_session_lifetime.total_seconds())   # default 2678400 (31 days)
try:
    data = s.loads(val, max_age=max_age)      # sessions.py:330-332
    return self.session_class(data)
except BadSignature:
    return self.session_class()              # sessions.py:334-335
```

itsdangerous `loads` iterates signers (current key, then fallbacks; `timed.py:194-220`), unsigns (verify HMAC over `payload.timestamp`, then compare base64 timestamps — rejecting if `age > max_age` or `age < 0` via `SignatureExpired`; `timed.py:141-149`), then `load_payload` base64-decodes, optional-zlib-decompresses, and calls **Flask's** `TaggedJSONSerializer.loads` → `_untag_scan(loads(value))` (`tag.py:325-327`). `_untag_scan` recursively descends dicts/lists and calls `untag` on each dict: a single-key dict whose key is a registered tag key is replaced by `tags[key].to_python(...)`; anything else passes through untouched (`tag.py:297-318`). The result is wrapped in `SecureCookieSession(data)` — a `CallbackDict` whose `on_update` sets `modified = True` (`sessions.py:57-80`).

Note the two distinct expiry concepts: the **cookie `Expires` attribute** (browser-side, only for `permanent` sessions, `sessions.py:369-370`) vs. the **signed timestamp `max_age`** (server-side, applied to *every* cookie load, permanent or not, `sessions.py:330-331`). A non-permanent session past `PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME` is still rejected by the server even though the browser may still send it.

---

## 3. Tampered cookie vs. expired cookie

**Tampered cookie (bad signature).** Any modification to payload or signature breaks the HMAC. itsdangerous raises `BadSignature` (or `BadTimeSignature("timestamp missing"/"Malformed timestamp")` which subclasses it, `exc.py:36`; `BadPayload` is *not* a `BadSignature` subclass — `exc.py:92` — but it only occurs after a signature already passed, so it can't fire for tampered input). `TimedSerializer.loads` tries all keys/fallbacks and re-raises the last exception (`timed.py:216-220`).

**Expired cookie.** The signature verifies fine, but `age > max_age` (or `age < 0`, a future timestamp, also rejected). itsdangerous raises `SignatureExpired`, which is `BadTimeSignature` → `BadSignature` (`exc.py:60, 36`). Critically, `TimedSerializer.loads` has `except SignatureExpired: raise` *before* the generic handler, so expiry is **not** retried against fallback keys and short-circuits immediately (`timed.py:213-215`).

**Identical handling in Flask.** `open_session` catches only `BadSignature`; since `SignatureExpired` is a subclass, both cases land in the same handler and return **`self.session_class()`** — a brand-new, empty `SecureCookieSession` (`sessions.py:332-335`). The request proceeds as if the user had no session: `flask.session` is an empty dict, `modified` starts `False` (`sessions.py:71`), and the view runs normally.

**Neither is surfaced as an application error.** No exception propagates to the app or error handlers; no logging; the client sees a normal 200 response, not a 400/401. The only observable signals: the session reads as empty, and since `modified` is `False`, the stale cookie is *not* proactively cleared (unless a view writes to the session, which sets `modified = True` and issues a fresh signed cookie on the next response). The two outcomes are indistinguishable to application code from "no cookie sent at all" — deliberate design: bad/expired cookies are treated as *no session* rather than as failures.

**One asymmetry worth noting:** because `TimedSerializer.loads` re-raises `SignatureExpired` without trying remaining fallback keys, a cookie signed with a *fallback* key that is also time-expired fails fast even if a newer key would... (irrelevant — signatures don't validate across keys anyway). More practically: expired-and-fallback-signed and expired-and-current-signed cookies behave identically in Flask's handler, but the underlying itsdangerous code paths differ (immediate re-raise vs. exhaust-all-keys-then-raise-last).

**Saving** (`src/flask/sessions.py:337-386`): an empty session deletes the cookie (if modified) or sets nothing (`src/flask/sessions.py:354-367`); otherwise, if `should_set_cookie` passes (`src/flask/sessions.py:233-245` — `modified`, or permanent plus `SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST`), it computes `expires` (`src/flask/sessions.py:223-231` — now + `PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME`, default 31 days at `src/flask/app.py:213`, only when `session.permanent`), then `val = self.get_signing_serializer(app).dumps(dict(session))` (`src/flask/sessions.py:373`) and issues `response.set_cookie(name, val, ...)` (`src/flask/sessions.py:374-383`), with `name` from `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` (default `"session"`, `src/flask/app.py:218`).

The dump chain: `dict(session)` → `TaggedJSONSerializer.dumps` recursively tags values and emits compact JSON via `flask.json.dumps(..., separators=(",", ":"))` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:321-323`; `flask.json.dumps` uses `current_app.json.dumps` when in an app context, `src/flask/json/__init__.py:40`, which defaults `ensure_ascii=True`, `sort_keys=True` per `src/flask/json/provider.py:176-179`). Then `URLSafeSerializerMixin.dump_payload` zlib-compresses if that is shorter and base64-encodes, prefixing `.` for compressed payloads (`itsdangerous/url_safe.py:55-69`). Finally `TimestampSigner.sign` appends `.` + base64(current unix timestamp) + `.` + base64(HMAC-SHA1 signature over payload+timestamp) (`itsdangerous/timed.py:45-52`, `itsdangerous/signer.py:222-224`). Cookie format: `<base64 payload>[.<timestamp>.<signature>]` (with a leading `.` when compressed).

**Non-standard types via the tagged serializer** — `TaggedJSONSerializer` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:219`) registers these default tags in order (`src/flask/json/tag.py:238-247`), documenting support for dict, tuple, bytes, Markup, UUID, datetime (`src/flask/json/tag.py:224-231`):

| Type | Tag key | JSON encoding | Restoration |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-item dict whose key is itself a tag key | `" di"` | `{"<tagkey>__": tagged_value}` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:93-116`) | key suffix `__` stripped (`tag.py:114-116`) — avoids ambiguity with a genuine single-key dict |
| tuple | `" t"` | list of tagged items (`src/flask/json/tag.py:133-145`) | `tuple(value)` (`tag.py:143-144`) |
| bytes | `" b"` | base64 ASCII string (`src/flask/json/tag.py:159-171`) | `b64decode` (`tag.py:169-170`) |
| `Markup` / any object with `__html__` | `" m"` | `str(value.__html__())` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:173-189`) | always `Markup(value)` (`tag.py:187-188`) |
| `uuid.UUID` | `" u"` | `value.hex` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:191-203`) | `UUID(value)` (`tag.py:201-202`) |
| `datetime` | `" d"` | RFC 2822 `http_date` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:205-217`) | werkzeug `parse_date` → timezone-aware datetime or `None` (`werkzeug/http.py:1022-1055`) |

Plain dicts and lists are handled by `PassDict`/`PassList`, which recurse into values without adding a tag (`src/flask/json/tag.py:119-157`); ordering matters because `TagDict`/`PassDict` are checked before lists (`tag()` iterates `self.order`, `src/flask/json/tag.py:289-294`). Extension is possible via `register()` including index insertion (`src/flask/json/tag.py:256-287`, example in module docstring).

**Restoring** (`src/flask/sessions.py:323-335`): the cookie value is read by name (`src/flask/sessions.py:327`); a missing/empty value yields a fresh empty `SecureCookieSession()` (`src/flask/sessions.py:328-329`). Otherwise `max_age = int(app.permanent_session_lifetime.total_seconds())` (`src/flask/sessions.py:330`; 31 days by default) and `data = s.loads(val, max_age=max_age)` (`src/flask/sessions.py:332`). The load chain: `TimedSerializer.loads` iterates unsigners (`itsdangerous/timed.py:185-220`), `TimestampSigner.unsign` verifies the signature over all keys and the age, then the payload is base64-decoded/decompressed (`itsdangerous/url_safe.py:30-53`) and `TaggedJSONSerializer.loads` parses JSON and runs `_untag_scan`, which recursively untags nested dicts/lists (`src/flask/json/tag.py:309-318`, keyed on single-key dicts whose key is a registered tag, `src/flask/json/tag.py:297-305`). The resulting dict is wrapped: `return self.session_class(data)` (`src/flask/sessions.py:333`) — a `SecureCookieSession`, a `CallbackDict` that flips `modified = True` on any mutation (`src/flask/sessions.py:57-80`).

## 3. Bad signature vs. expired timestamp

**Tampered cookie** (signature mismatch): `Signer.unsign` fails on every key (tried newest-first, `itsdangerous/signer.py:236`, raising `BadSignature` at `itsdangerous/signer.py:256`); `TimestampSigner.unsign` re-raises this as a `BadTimeSignature` carrying the payload and `date_signed` (`itsdangerous/timed.py:130`; class at `itsdangerous/exc.py:36`). In `TimedSerializer.loads` the `BadSignature` is caught per-signer and retried against the remaining keys (`itsdangerous/timed.py:213-218`) — so with fallback keys configured, an old-key-signed cookie still loads, which is exactly the rotation path in `tests/test_basic.py:413-418`. When all keys fail, the last exception is raised (`itsdangerous/timed.py:220`).

**Expired cookie** (valid signature, old timestamp): the signature verifies, but `age > max_age` (or a negative age, i.e., a future timestamp) raises `SignatureExpired` with `date_signed` (`itsdangerous/timed.py:141-153`; class at `itsdangerous/exc.py:60`, a subclass of `BadTimeSignature` → `BadSignature`). Crucially, `TimedSerializer.loads` re-raises `SignatureExpired` immediately without trying other keys, because the cookie was legitimately signed but is simply stale (`itsdangerous/timed.py:213-216`, "The signature was unsigned successfully but was expired. Do not try the next signer."). This is the one behavioral difference between the two cases: tampering exhausts the key list; expiry short-circuits on the first key that validates. Note this server-side expiry is independent of the cookie's browser-side `Expires` attribute — the itsdangerous timestamp is embedded on every cookie (`itsdangerous/timed.py:45-52`), while the `Expires` attribute is only set for permanent sessions (`src/flask/sessions.py:223-231`).

**Resulting session object and error surfacing — identical for both**: because `BadTimeSignature` and `SignatureExpired` are both subclasses of `BadSignature` (`itsdangerous/exc.py:36`, `exc.py:60`), Flask's single handler in `open_session` catches both: `except BadSignature: return self.session_class()` (`src/flask/sessions.py:334-335`). The request proceeds with a fresh, empty `SecureCookieSession` — `new` is hard-coded `False` and `modified` starts `False` (`src/flask/sessions.py:71`), so no `Set-Cookie` is emitted unless the view modifies the session (empty + modified deletes the cookie, `src/flask/sessions.py:354-357`; otherwise `should_set_cookie` gates it, `src/flask/sessions.py:233-245`). Neither condition is surfaced to the application: no exception propagates, no error page, no log entry from this code path, and the two cases are indistinguishable to view code. The empty-session outcome for an unusable signature is confirmed by `tests/test_basic.py:410-412` (rotating the secret key away from the signing key yields `{}` with no error). The only related error path is different: no secret key at all produces a `NullSession` whose writes raise `RuntimeError` (`src/flask/sessions.py:89-96`) — but that requires a missing key, not a bad or stale cookie. (One edge case outside these two conditions: a cookie whose signature is valid but payload is corrupt JSON raises `BadPayload`, which subclasses `BadData`, not `BadSignature`, and would propagate as a server error — it is not caught here.)

## 1. How the signing serializer is constructed

The default session interface is `SecureCookieSessionInterface`, assigned as `Flask.session_interface` at `src/flask/app.py:248`. Its class attributes define the signing scheme (`src/flask/sessions.py:284-301`):

- **Salt**: `salt = "cookie-session"` (`src/flask/sessions.py:291`). This is applied on top of the secret key so the same key produces different signatures for different purposes (it replaces itsdangerous' default `b"itsdangerous"` salt, `itsdangerous/serializer.py` in the installed `itsdangerous` package at `/home/lamim/.cache/uv/archive-v0/lZ5zOjAj4cfTPYvP/`).
- **Digest**: `digest_method = staticmethod(_lazy_sha1)` (`src/flask/sessions.py:293`). `_lazy_sha1` (`src/flask/sessions.py:276-281`) deliberately defers `hashlib.sha1` to runtime so FIPS builds that lack SHA-1 don't fail at import time before the developer can configure another digest.
- **Key derivation**: `key_derivation = "hmac"` (`src/flask/sessions.py:296`), overriding itsdangerous' default `django-concat` (`itsdangerous/signer.py:126-127`). Under `"hmac"` the per-context signing key is `HMAC-SHA1(secret_key, salt)` (`itsdangerous/signer.py:206-209`), rather than a hash concatenation.
- **Serializer**: `serializer = session_json_serializer`, a module-level `TaggedJSONSerializer()` (`src/flask/sessions.py:273, 300`), and `session_class = SecureCookieSession` (`src/flask/sessions.py:301`).

`get_signing_serializer(app)` (`src/flask/sessions.py:303-321`) builds a fresh `URLSafeTimedSerializer` per call:

1. Returns `None` if `app.secret_key` is falsy (`src/flask/sessions.py:304-305`); `secret_key` is a `ConfigAttribute` over the `SECRET_KEY` config, default `None` (`src/flask/sansio/app.py:213`, `src/flask/app.py:211`).
2. Key list: values from `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` (default `None`, `src/flask/app.py:212`) are extended in first (`src/flask/sessions.py:309-310`), then the current `app.secret_key` is appended last (`src/flask/sessions.py:312`). itsdangerous treats the list as oldest-to-newest: the **last** (current) key signs (`itsdangerous/signer.py:186-188`, `itsdangerous/serializer.py:243`), while verification tries keys newest-first via `reversed(self.secret_keys)` (`itsdangerous/signer.py:236-239`). This is what makes key rotation work, verified by `tests/test_basic.py:393-417`.
3. It returns `URLSafeTimedSerializer(keys, salt=self.salt, serializer=self.serializer, signer_kwargs={"key_derivation": self.key_derivation, "digest_method": self.digest_method})` (`src/flask/sessions.py:313-321`). `URLSafeTimedSerializer` is `URLSafeSerializerMixin + TimedSerializer` (`itsdangerous/url_safe.py:79`), so it signs with a `TimestampSigner` (`itsdangerous/timed.py:36`) whose signature is `HMAC-SHA1(derived_key, value + "." + timestamp)` (`itsdangerous/signer.py:62-63`, `itsdangerous/timed.py:46-52`).

## 2. Serialization into the cookie and restoration

**Saving (session → cookie).** `finalize_request` calls `save_session` unless the session is a null session (`src/flask/app.py:1415-1416`). In `save_session` (`src/flask/sessions.py:337-385`):

- A `Vary: Cookie` header is added if the session was accessed (`src/flask/sessions.py:348-350`); `accessed` is set by the request context's `session` property (`src/flask/ctx.py:401-403`).
- An empty session deletes the cookie (if modified) or writes nothing (`src/flask/sessions.py:351-365`).
- Otherwise the cookie is written if `should_set_cookie` is true: `modified` or (permanent and `SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST`, default `True`, `src/flask/app.py:225`) (`src/flask/sessions.py:233-247`, `src/flask/sessions.py:369-370`).
- `expires` is `None` for non-permanent sessions or `now + PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME` (default 31 days, `src/flask/app.py:213`) for permanent ones (`src/flask/sessions.py:219-232`, `src/flask/sessions.py:372`).
- The value is `get_signing_serializer(app).dumps(dict(session))` (`src/flask/sessions.py:373`), set via `response.set_cookie` with the name from `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` (default `"session"`, `src/flask/app.py:218`) and the usual domain/path/secure/samesite/httponly/partitioned attributes (`src/flask/sessions.py:374-384`).

The dumps pipeline: `TaggedJSONSerializer.dumps` tags the value recursively and JSON-dumps compactly with `separators=(",", ":")` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:321-323`; `flask.json.dumps` routes through `current_app.json.dumps` when a context is active, `src/flask/json/__init__.py` — during `save_session` it is — applying `sort_keys=True`/`ensure_ascii=True` defaults from `src/flask/json/provider.py:176-179`). The cookie thus looks like `payload[.timestamp].signature`, e.g. `eyJhIjoxfQ.Zx2K5w.signature`.

**Non-standard Python value types in the tagged serializer** (`src/flask/json/tag.py:226-232` and the tag classes):

| Type | Tag key | JSON form | Restore |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tuple` | `" t"` | list (`src/flask/json/tag.py:133-145`) | `tuple(value)` |
| `bytes` | `" b"` | base64 ASCII string (`src/flask/json/tag.py:159-169`) | `b64decode` |
| `markupsafe.Markup` (anything with `__html__`) | `" m"` | `str(value.__html__())` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:173-187`) | `Markup(value)` |
| `uuid.UUID` | `" u"` | `value.hex` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:191-201`) | `UUID(value)` |
| `datetime` | `" d"` | HTTP date string via `http_date` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:205-215`) | werkzeug `parse_date` |
| 1-item dict whose key collides with a tag key | `" di"` | key suffixed with `__` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:93-117`) | strips `__` |

Plain dicts and lists are handled by `PassDict`/`PassList`, which just tag items recursively (`src/flask/json/tag.py:119-157`). Tag order comes from `default_tags` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:238-248`); tagging picks the first tag whose `check()` matches (`src/flask/json/tag.py:289-295`). Round-tripping of all of these (including the `" di"` collision case) is tested in `tests/test_json_tag.py:12-41`.

**Restoring (cookie → session).** `AppContext.push` opens the session (or does so lazily on first access) via `_get_session` (`src/flask/ctx.py:381-392`, `439`, `399-403`); if `open_session` returns `None` (no secret key), a `NullSession` is created instead (`src/flask/ctx.py:390-391`). `open_session` (`src/flask/sessions.py:323-335`):

1. Reads `request.cookies.get("session")` (`src/flask/sessions.py:327`). Missing/empty → fresh empty `SecureCookieSession()` (`:328-329`).
2. `max_age = int(app.permanent_session_lifetime.total_seconds())` (`src/flask/sessions.py:330`) — always applied, whether or not the session is permanent.
3. `s.loads(val, max_age=max_age)` (`src/flask/sessions.py:332`). itsdangerous verifies the HMAC against each key (current first, then fallbacks), splits off the base64 timestamp, rejects ages beyond `max_age` (`itsdangerous/timed.py:138-153`), then `load_payload` base64-decodes, zlib-decompresses if prefixed with `.`, UTF-8 decodes, and calls `TaggedJSONSerializer.loads` (`itsdangerous/url_safe.py:23-52`). `loads` → `_untag_scan` recursively untag dicts/lists, converting any 1-key dict whose key is a registered tag key back to the Python type (`src/flask/json/tag.py:297-318`, `325-327`).
4. Success: `SecureCookieSession(data)` — a werkzeug `CallbackDict` whose `on_update` sets `modified = True` on any change (`src/flask/sessions.py:57-80`, class default `modified = False` at `:71`).

## 3. Bad signature vs. expired timestamp

Both conditions funnel into the same handler. `open_session` wraps loads in `try/except BadSignature: return self.session_class()` (`src/flask/sessions.py:331-335`).

**Tampered cookie (bad signature).** No key (current or fallback) verifies the HMAC. itsdangerous raises `BadSignature` from `Signer.unsign` (`itsdangerous/signer.py:258`), surfaced (after timestamp parsing) as a `BadTimeSignature` subclass of `BadSignature` (`itsdangerous/timed.py:130`). The payload is never deserialized. Note that a cookie signed with an *unknown* key behaves identically: `tests/test_basic.py:410-411` shows changing the secret key makes the session "can't be loaded and appears empty".

**Expired cookie (valid signature, stale timestamp).** The signature verifies, but `age > max_age` (or a negative/future timestamp) raises `SignatureExpired` (`itsdangerous/timed.py:141-153`). `SignatureExpired` is a subclass of `BadTimeSignature`, which is a subclass of `BadSignature` (`itsdangerous/exc.py:60-62, 36-38, 22-24`), so Flask's single `except BadSignature` catches it too. One real behavioral difference inside itsdangerous: `TimedSerializer.loads` re-raises `SignatureExpired` immediately without trying the remaining fallback keys, because the signature was valid, just old (`itsdangerous/timed.py:208-211`). So an expired cookie signed with an old fallback key still expires on its own timestamp rather than being retried.

**Resulting session object — identical in both cases**: a fresh, empty `SecureCookieSession()` (`src/flask/sessions.py:335`) with `modified = False` (`:71`), `new = False` hard-coded (`:39`, per the class docstring at `:62-66` it "cannot reliably track whether a session is new (vs. empty)"), `accessed = False` until the `session` proxy touches it (`src/flask/ctx.py:402`).

**Neither condition is an application error.** The exception is silently swallowed at `src/flask/sessions.py:334-335`; nothing is logged in Flask itself, no error page or status code results, and no signal is sent. The request proceeds with an anonymous session; if the view then modifies it, `modified` becomes true and `should_set_cookie` writes a fresh cookie (`src/flask/sessions.py:233-247`, `373-384`), and `Vary: Cookie` is added because the session was accessed (`:348-350`). All evidence gathered. Here is the trace.

# Session lifecycle: no usable secret key, and save at end of request

## 1. `open_session` returning `None` → null session

**Where the fallback happens.** The session is opened lazily via `AppContext._get_session()` (src/flask/ctx.py:381). If the interface's `open_session` returns `None`, the context substitutes a null session (src/flask/ctx.py:386-392):

```python
if self._session is None:
    si = self.app.session_interface
    self._session = si.open_session(self.app, self.request)
    if self._session is None:
        self._session = si.make_null_session(self.app)
```

This is invoked eagerly when a request context is pushed, deliberately before URL matching so a custom `open_session` can use the request context (src/flask/ctx.py:437-439), matching the documented contract "at the beginning of each request, after pushing the request context, before matching the URL" (src/flask/sessions.py:250-252).

**When `None` occurs with the default interface.** `SecureCookieSessionInterface.get_signing_serializer` returns `None` when `app.secret_key` is falsy (src/flask/sessions.py:303-305), and `open_session` propagates that as `None` (src/flask/sessions.py:324-326). So "no usable secret key" is exactly the trigger.

**What the null session is.** `make_null_session` instantiates `null_session_class`, which defaults to `NullSession` (src/flask/sessions.py:141, 160). `NullSession` subclasses `SecureCookieSession` and "will still allow read-only access to the empty session but fail on setting" (src/flask/sessions.py:83-86). Every mutating method is bound to `_fail`, which raises `RuntimeError("The session is unavailable because no secret key was set...")` (src/flask/sessions.py:89-96):

```python
__setitem__ = __delitem__ = clear = pop = popitem = update = setdefault = _fail
```

Permitted operations are therefore the read-only dict interface inherited from `SecureCookieSession`/`CallbackDict`: `get()`, `__getitem__`, `__contains__`, iteration, `len()` — all against an empty mapping. Reads like `session.get("user")` return `None` silently; even the `permanent` property getter works since it only calls `self.get("_permanent", False)` (src/flask/sessions.py:28-30), though the setter would fail because it writes `self["_permanent"]` (src/flask/sessions.py:32-34).

**Is it saved?** No. `is_null_session` type-checks against `null_session_class` and is documented as "Null sessions are not asked to be saved" (src/flask/sessions.py:162-169). In `process_response`, saving is gated: `if not self.session_interface.is_null_session(ctx._get_session()): self.session_interface.save_session(...)` (src/flask/app.py:1415-1416), and the `save_session` docstring confirms "It is skipped if `is_null_session` returns `True`" (src/flask/sessions.py:266-268). So a null session never writes a cookie (and never adds `Vary: Cookie`, since that logic lives inside `save_session`, which is never called for it).

## 2. `Vary` header, cookie deletion, and cookie setting

All three behaviors live in `SecureCookieSessionInterface.save_session` (src/flask/sessions.py:337-385), which first gathers cookie attributes (name, domain, path, secure, partitioned, samesite, httponly; src/flask/sessions.py:338-346).

**`Vary` header.** `response.vary.add("Cookie")` is added unconditionally when `session.accessed` is true, before any empty/non-empty branching (src/flask/sessions.py:348-350). `accessed` is set to `True` by the `AppContext.session` property every time the session is touched through the request context, including the global `session` proxy (src/flask/ctx.py:396-403; documented at src/flask/sessions.py:46-55). Additionally, both the delete-cookie path and the set-cookie path add `Vary: Cookie` again (src/flask/sessions.py:365, 385) — idempotent since it's a header set, but it means those outcomes guarantee the header even if `accessed` were somehow false.

**Empty modified session → cookie deleted.** If `not session` (empty dict) and `session.modified`, `response.delete_cookie(...)` is issued with the same attribute set (domain, path, secure, partitioned, samesite, httponly) so the browser actually removes the right cookie (src/flask/sessions.py:354-364), then `Vary: Cookie` is added and the method returns (src/flask/sessions.py:365-367). Note this deletion path does *not* consult `should_set_cookie` — the docstring confirms "This check is usually skipped if the session was deleted" (src/flask/sessions.py:240-241). If the session is empty but *not* modified, the method simply returns without touching cookies (comment at src/flask/sessions.py:352-353; return at 367) — an untouched empty session produces no `Set-Cookie` at all, only the possible accessed-based `Vary`.

**Non-empty session → new cookie.** For a non-empty session, `should_set_cookie` is consulted (src/flask/sessions.py:369-370; return early if false).
